abstract: Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is an increasingly utilized minimally invasive treatment for intractable epilepsy that enables focal destruction of epileptogenic tissue. Despite increasing clinical adoption, the acute network-level consequences of focal tissue ablation remain poorly understood. Previous studies have identified the emergence of slow, sleep-like activity following RFA, but have largely focused on low-frequency oscillations. Here, we investigated distributed cortical reorganization immediately following ablation using aperiodic features derived from scalp EEG. Six patients with medically refractory epilepsy underwent clinically indicated amygdala RFA (3R/3L). Scalp EEG was recorded before and after ablation. To facilitate group-level comparisons, recordings were reflected into a common lesion hemisphere such that right-sided electrodes were treated as ipsilateral to the lesion. Power spectra were computed across electrodes and parameterized to quantify changes in aperiodic exponent and offset following ablation. Following amygdala RFA, scalp EEG exhibited marked hemispheric asymmetries in aperiodic activity. Aperiodic exponent increased most prominently in the contralesional hemisphere, with maximal effects observed over frontotemporal and central electrodes (F7, T7, and C3). In contrast, increases in exponent in the ipsilesional hemisphere were smaller and largely confined to frontal regions. Aperiodic offset exhibited the opposite hemispheric distribution, with the largest increases localized to the ipsilateral hemisphere and centered over frontocentral electrodes (F4, C4, and Cz). Together, these findings reveal hemispheric-specific alterations in aperiodic activity following focal amygdala ablation. A highly localized lesion produced spatially organized changes in large-scale neural dynamics detectable by scalp EEG. Quantifying these aperiodic signatures may provide a scalable biomarker for measuring network reorganization following focal brain lesions and other causal perturbations of the human brain.

abstract: Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) severely impairs quality of life through chronic pelvic pain and lower urinary tract symptoms. We previously identified lumbosacral spinal Trpc4⁺ neurons as a population that gates visceral pain and regulates bladder function in cyclophosphamide-induced cystitis. However, the intraspinal circuit mechanisms by which Trpc4⁺ neurons coordinate lower urinary tract output remain unclear. To address this, we examined synaptic connectivity from Trpc4⁺ dorsal gray commissure (DGC) neurons onto two major spinal output populations: lumbosacral preganglionic neurons (LS-PGNs), which regulate bladder contraction, and dorsolateral motor neurons (DL-MNs), which control external urethral sphincter (EUS) muscle activity. Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings combined with optogenetic terminal stimulation revealed target-specific synaptic organization. LS-PGNs received inhibitory-biased synaptic input from Trpc4⁺ DGC neurons, whereas DL-MNs received excitatory-biased input. These findings suggest that Trpc4⁺ spinal interneurons coordinate lower urinary tract function by differentially regulating bladder contraction and EUS muscle activity. Target-specific synaptic bias onto LS-PGNs and DL-MNs may explain how Trpc4⁺ neuron manipulation modulates cystitis-associated voiding dysfunction and visceral pain.

abstract:
Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) has been shown to improve working memory performance, but the physiological mechanism underlying this cognitive benefit remains unclear. This mechanistic gap limits the targeted use of taVNS as a cognitive intervention. Successful working memory requires efficient maintenance of task information while regulating sensory input from both the external environment and the body. Improved working memory could therefore reflect increased arousal, enhanced processing of task-relevant stimuli, and reduced interference from internal bodily signals. Distinguishing among these possibilities is important because each mechanism predicts a different cognitive context in which taVNS may be most effective.
The vagal afferents convey interoceptive signals from the body and engage brainstem-cortical systems involved in arousal and attention. We therefore ask whether taVNS improves working memory by modulating the balance between interoceptive and exteroceptive attention. To answer this question, we quantified stimulus-evoked potentials (SEPs) and heart-evoked potentials (HEPs) during an N-back working memory task and compared these responses between active taVNS and sham stimulation.
We recorded eye movements, electroencephalogram (EEG), and electrocardiogram (ECG) from 20 healthy participants who completed N-back tasks during baseline, sham stimulation, and active taVNS sessions. We developed a template-matching approach to separate EEG components associated with stimulation artifacts, eye movements, and cardiac activity. We quantified SEPs and HEPs at the sensor level and estimated their cortical sources. We assessed taVNS effects on SEPs and HEPs using time-resolved statistical mapping, threshold-free cluster enhancement, and cluster-based permutation testing. We further explored whether SEP and HEP morphology were associated with working memory performance.
We found robust stimulus-evoked responses and detectable heart-evoked responses during the N-back task. Active taVNS reduced SEPs relative to sham. HEP modulation was weaker but showed a similar direction, with reduced cardiac-related cortical responses during active taVNS. These findings suggest that taVNS does not simply amplify sensory responses during working memory. Instead, active taVNS may shift the balance between interoceptive and exteroceptive attention toward a more efficient task-maintenance state.

abstract: Learning in variable environments requires animals to use past experience to guide future actions, yet how the brain forms episodic memories from information about when, where, and what occurred, and how it uses these memories for prediction, remains elusive. Here, we investigate whether and how representational drift in hippocampal CA1, gradual changes in neural activity patterns across repeated recording sessions over days to weeks, support the formation and retrieval of time-stamped episodic memories. Motivated by previous work on the distributed coding of temporal history across multiple decay rates, we developed a computational model in which representational drift with distributed drift rates binds temporal context to neural activity. This mechanism allows reward or threat episodes to be stored and later retrieved across multiple timescales for prospective prediction. We then tested a key assumption of the model: that the time constants of representational drift are distributed across neurons. Across datasets, CA1 neurons showed broadly distributed drift time constants, with weak but significant stability of these time constants across environments and over time. These results suggest that representational drift may provide temporal information to episodic memories and support prospective learning through distributed mechanisms.

abstract: Organisms rely on neural circuits that monitor internal danger to adaptively regulate behavior. However, in conditions of persistent somatic stress such as chemotherapy, these responses can become maladaptive, producing debilitating amotivation and fatigue that limit quality of life and treatment adherence. Here we identify a chemotherapy-responsive danger-sensing circuit that drives amotivation and fatigue. Systemic chemotherapy-induced cellular stress selectively elevates circulating GDF15, a danger cytokine detected by GFRAL-expressing neurons in the area postrema (ArP). These neurons engage parallel relays through the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) and the parabrachial nucleus (PBN) to converge on midbrain inhibitory nodes, suppressing mesolimbic dopamine release and attenuating effort-based motivation. Direct optogenetic and chemogenetic activation of this circuit is sufficient to reproduce these dopaminergic and motivational deficits, and recombinant GDF15 phenocopies these effects. Conversely, silencing ArP GFRAL neurons or restoration of dopamine tone via chemogenetics or pharmacology rescues motivational drive following chemotherapy. Thus, a conserved GDF15-GFRAL danger circuit links somatic stress to reduced behavioral drive, revealing a neural mechanism through which internal injury suppresses motivation.

abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is increasingly recognized as a disorder of early immunometabolic dysfunction, yet exactly how amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology reshapes brain metabolism and how that metabolic impairment shapes pathogenesis remains poorly understood. Although late-stage disease is associated with cerebral hypometabolism, recent evidence suggests that amyloid pathology initially drives hypermetabolic changes, specifically involving the glycolytic end product lactate. The drivers and consequences of these early metabolic adaptations, however, remain unclear. This project aims to characterize brain lactate metabolism relative to amyloid plaques in the APP/PS1 mouse model and human AD tissue and test whether blocking lactate metabolism alters Aβ-related pathology, metabolism, and neuroinflammation. We found that amyloid plaque deposition is associated with progressive increases in brain lactate in APP/PS1 mice. In vivo microdialysis demonstrated that interstitial fluid (ISF) lactate increases by 50% while ISF glucose decreases by 25% with plaques. Stable isotope-resolved metabolomics revealed widespread metabolic reprogramming characterized by enhanced glycolysis and reduced tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediates and neurotransmitter biosynthesis. Lactate dehydrogenase A (Ldha), the enzyme required for lactate generation, is highly enriched in the peri-plaque microenvironment and preferentially localized to diffuse Aβ deposits rather than the dense core of amyloid plaques. Spatial and transcriptomic analyses identified microglia as a major source of lactate within the amyloid-bearing brain; specifically, Ldha is enriched within peri-plaque microglia in APP/PS1 mice. Furthermore, single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomic analyses reveal upregulated LDHA in microglia from clinical AD patients, particularly in a distinct microglial population associated with innate immune signaling and cytokine production. Critically, this immunometabolic signature was reversible. Pharmacological inhibition of lactate dehydrogenase in APP/PS1 mice with stiripentol, an FDA-approved anti-seizure medication, reduced ISF lactate and Aβ levels and selectively depleted peri-plaque microglia, including Cd68⁺ and Clec7a⁺ populations. Ongoing studies are further characterizing the effects of Aβ pathology on microglia mitochondrial function and investigating the functional role of microglial-derived lactate utilizing a novel microglia-specific Ldha knockout mouse. These data support a model in which microglial lactate links altered brain metabolism to neuroinflammation and amyloid pathology.

abstract: Neural activity is stabilized by homeostatic mechanisms that regulate features of single-neuron and population dynamics around set-points. We recently found that tau-mediated neurodegeneration disrupts population-level set-points while sparing the set-points of the constituent individual neurons. This immediately raises two questions, 1) whether disruption of population-level set-points generalizes across molecularly distinct models of disease, and 2) whether it is restricted to selectively vulnerable circuits associated with cognitive function. We analyzed chronic, multi-region in vivo electrophysiological recordings from APP/PS1 and wild-type (WT) at young (≤4 months) and old (≥12 months) ages. Single units were recorded simultaneously from retrosplenial cortex (RSC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), CA1 hippocampus, and primary visual cortex (V1), enabling within-animal comparison of selectively vulnerable regions of the default mode network with a primary sensory region. Amyloid progression produced age- and circuit-specific alterations in firing rate and spike-time variability, which were significantly impaired in ACC and CA1, while V1 was spared. Population-level set-points were also progressively disrupted. Multiple complementary measures of criticality—a network regime characterized by scale free dynamics—showed age- and state-dependent impairments selectively within cognitively vulnerable circuits while consistently sparing V1. Thus, amyloid pathology progressively disrupts neuronal homeostatic set-points in a circuit-specific manner, with convergent population-level deficits concentrated in cognitively vulnerable circuits despite widespread amyloid burden. These findings support loss of network homeostasis as a generalizable functional consequence of neurodegenerative disease processes.

abstract:
Background: Alzheimer disease (AD) is characterized by amyloid-beta plaque and tau tangle accumulation, with regional pathology correlating with clinical presentation. Atypical presentations are often missed in their early stages, making characterization of this pathological spread critical. Autosomal dominant AD (ADAD) is a familial form caused by genetic mutations that affect amyloid-beta production and offers a unique model to observe AD pathophysiology that's free from the confounding influence of age-related copathologies common in sporadic AD. Spatiotemporal heterogeneity exists in sporadic AD, but the specific spatiotemporal subtypes of amyloid spread in ADAD remain poorly understood.
Method: The data-driven Subtype and Stage Inference (SuStaIn) algorithm uses cross-sectional biomarker data to identify subtypes with distinct stages of disease progression. SuStaIn was applied to PiB-PET scans from 213 mutation carriers and 149 non-carriers from the Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network. Brain data were summarized into 5 regions: frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, and basal ganglia. Models were compared using maximum likelihood estimation and cross-validation information criterion.
Results: We identified 3 distinct patterns of amyloid spatiotemporal spread. Subtype 1 exhibits early deposition in the occipital lobe (then parietal, frontal, temporal, and basal ganglia) (1a). Subtype 2 exhibits early deposition in the basal ganglia (then frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital) (1b). Subtypes 1 and 2 capture atypical patterns of amyloid spread, while Subtype 3 captures the canonical pattern, with early deposition in the frontal lobe (then parietal, temporal, occipital, and basal ganglia) (1c).
Conclusion: Amyloid pathological heterogeneity is detectable in ADAD and can be subtyped into 3 distinct patterns of spatiotemporal spread. Future work will investigate biological drivers of this heterogeneity to improve biomarker sensitivity, personalize patient care, and optimize clinical trials based on biological profile.

abstract:
Neuroinflammation is increasingly recognized as a key contributor to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathogenesis, yet fluid biomarkers that reflect immune activation and predict disease progression remain incompletely characterized. We investigated associations between cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) immune activation markers, established AD biomarkers, and clinical progression in older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and probable AD dementia. Participants included 131 individuals with MCI and 69 with AD dementia enrolled in Mayo Clinic aging and dementia research cohorts. CSF levels of 358 immune-related proteins were quantified using proximity extension assays and analyzed in relation to demographic factors, APOE genotype, and established AD biomarkers. Longitudinal analyses were performed in 110 participants with MCI followed for a median of 3.9 years to assess progression to dementia (Clinical Dementia Rating global score ≥1).
Age, sex, and APOE ε4 status were associated with distinct immune marker profiles, with APOE ε4 carriers exhibiting higher CSF SNAP-25 levels. Immune activation markers demonstrated strong positive
associations with markers of synaptic dysfunction and neurodegeneration, including neurogranin, SNAP-25, and YKL-40. Among all immune markers examined, AGER showed associations across the full panel of established AD biomarkers. During follow-up, 22 participants progressed from MCI to dementia. Higher CSF glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) levels were associated with increased risk of progression, while lower levels of GALNT3, PCDH1, and CD48 showed suggestive associations with conversion to dementia. Exploratory analyses further identified the ANGPTL4/PCDH1 ratio as a potential predictor of clinical progression.
These findings demonstrate that CSF immune activation markers are closely linked to core AD-related biological processes and clinical outcomes. GFAP and selected immune-related proteins may serve as candidate biomarkers for predicting progression from MCI to dementia and could contribute to stage-specific risk stratification across the AD continuum.

abstract: Background: White matter is often treated as a PET reference or normalization region. Yet, its biological properties, age-related variability, and sensitivity to partial-volume effects remain uncertain. We developed a multimodal PET framework to estimate deep white matter metabolism while limiting grey matter spill-in and ventricular contamination, and examined white matter signal changes with aging in cognitively healthy older adults. Exclusion criteria included a CDR greater than zero, a moderate or severe white matter disease burden (Fazekas score), and, for participants above age 55, amyloid-positivity through testing. Methods: [18F] FDG, [15O] H2O, [15O] CO, and [15O] O2 PET data were collected on Siemens Biograph Vision PET/CT scanner. These tracers measure glucose consumption, cerebral blood flow (CBF), cerebral blood volume, and enable computation of the oxygen extraction fraction (OEF), and cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2). Subject-specific white matter masks were generated from FreeSurfer tissue segmentation and then subsequent distance from grey matter and distance from ventricles maps were created. Deep white matter was defined using grey matter partial-volume effect simulations, non-parametric flexible modeling, and distance-from-grey-matter (7.5 mm-10 mm)-and-ventricle (>5mm) criteria. For each modality, grey matter and deep white matter mean values were extracted, and grey-to-white matter ratios were computed. Age associations were tested with sex-adjusted models. Results: The pipeline consistently identified a deep white matter region across participants. Across FDG, CBF, CBV, rOEF, and rCMRO2, grey matter and white matter showed age-related patterns. Specifically, non-partial-volume corrected analyses suggested that FDG, CBF, and rCMRO2 grey-to-white matter ratios decreased with advancing age. Ongoing analyses will incorporate partial-volume correction to account for cortical thinning and kinetic modeling to quantitatively evaluate white matter metabolism. Conclusion: This project establishes a subject-specific, distance-based approach for measuring deep white matter PET data across metabolic modalities. The findings carry implications for PET reference-region selection and interpretation of white matter signals in aging and neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases. Ongoing analyses investigate grey-to-white matter ratios of brain metabolism and blood flow as a function of age.

abstract: The dorsolateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) of the thalamus relays visual information from the retina to the visual cortex and is essential for conscious vision. In blinding diseases such as glaucoma, the human dLGN undergoes significant atrophy, characterized by reduced anatomical volume and decreases in thalamocortical cell quantity and soma size. While these changes have been well-studied in non-human primate and feline models, they remain poorly characterized in mice, thus hindering the development of a murine model of transneuronal degeneration in the dLGN. Here, we employed a monocular optic nerve crush to assess degeneration in the dLGN. At either three or six months post crush, cholera toxin-B (CTB) was injected into the vitreous body of the eye as an anterograde tracer to visualize the region. Using serial sectioning and subsequent volumetric reconstructions of the dLGN, the volume and density of neurons, microglia, and astrocytes in the dLGN ipsilateral and contralateral to the injury, as well as in eye-specific subregions within each dLGN were quantified to characterize transneuronal responses following injury. Monocular optic nerve crush resulted in a substantial reduction in volume of the dLGN receiving input from the crushed eye, with a continued, but smaller, decrease at six months. These changes were reflected in both neuronal and microglial populations, as neuronal cell numbers decreased within crushed-eye subregions while microglial cell numbers increased, producing corresponding shifts in density. These results establish a quantitative baseline for ongoing preservation studies aimed at reducing the severity of transneuronal degeneration following optic nerve injury.

abstract: Endometriosis pain is debilitating for many of the 10% of women affected by the disease, yet few studies evaluate the mechanisms underlying this chronic pelvic pain. Current treatments are often inadequate, necessitating surgical resection of endometrial-like lesions to manage symptoms. Unfortunately, lesions and pain often recur. Clinical studies suggest that lesion innervation, rather than disease stage, correlates with pain severity; however, the identity and functional properties of these lesion-innervating neurons remain undefined. We utilized a syngeneic mouse model of the disease to characterize dorsal root ganglia (DRG) sensory neurons that innervate peritoneal lesions or nearby control peritoneum. We found that these lesions are preferentially innervated by small-diameter, IB4-positive sensory neurons, suggesting neuronal growth factor receptor signaling. Patch clamp electrophysiology of lesion-innervating neurons revealed that these cells are hyperexcitable compared to size-matched control DRG neurons. To translate these findings, we performed proteomics of clinical lesion samples stratified by patient-reported pain. We identified an enrichment of many neurotrophic factors, including Glial Cell Line-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (GDNF), in lesions from patients who reported severe pain. GDNF aligned characteristically with the stroma of endometrial lesions, and its receptor, GFRα1, expression levels correlated with levels of peripherin-positive axons. Histological analyses confirmed that stromal GDNF expression, as well as that of peripherin and GFRα1, is associated with clinical pain. These data provide functional evidence that lesions drive nociceptor excitability and implicate the stromal GDNF-GFRα1 signaling axis in the recruitment of nociceptors to lesions. Our results identify this axis and suggest that it may be a disease modifying target to provide novel, non-hormonal strategies for the management or recurrence of endometriosis pain.

abstract: It has been well-established that the early childhood environment impacts later physical and mental health. Environmental measures such as childhood stress, family dynamics, and neighborhood context can be traced in functional networks in older adolescents; however, it is unclear when these patterns first emerge. In this study, we examine the relationship between neighborhood environment, perinatal health, and functional networks in infancy. We utilized data from the first postnatal visit (0-1 month old) of the Healthy Brain and Child Development (HBCD) study. Area deprivation index (ADI), a measure of neighborhood socioeconomic disadvantage, was acquired through geocoded address data, and birthweight, a predictor of infant health, was acquired in a survey collected at the first postnatal visit. Connectivity data were generated from minimally preprocessed resting-state fMRI data using fMRIPrep and XCPD pipelines. After motion scrubbing, a minimum of 8 minutes of low-motion (<0.2mm FD) data was used for each participant. Finally, vertexwise time series were parcellated using the Gordon atlas, and functional connectivity between regions was calculated using Pearson correlation and fisher z-transformed. Ridge regression was used to fit whole-brain prediction models. Model training was performed using a 5x5 nested cross-validation scheme. Feature-wise confound removal of sex and age was performed using linear regression within each training fold, and the confound models were applied to held-out test data to prevent data leakage. Regression weights were Haufe-transformed, and out-of-sample model performance was assessed for significance against a permutation-based null distribution (1000 repeats). ADI (N=487) and birthweight (N=642) were both predicted out-of-sample with moderate accuracy (ADI r=0.405; birthweight r=0.245). Predictions were statistically significant for birthweight (p=0.001) and trended towards significance for ADI (p=0.083). Haufe-transformed feature weights for both ADI and infant birthweight were highest in sensorimotor regions, where ADI showed a negative correlation, and birthweight showed a positive correlation with FC. ADI and birthweight were not significantly correlated in this sample (r=-0.056, p=0.22). These neural patterns support findings in adolescents, suggesting that environmental context is correlated with neural activity already in early childhood and that these relationships may show continuity across the lifespan. A better understanding of how the environment shapes functional network development may provide valuable insight into the pathophysiology of psychiatric disorders.

abstract: Symptomatic knee osteoarthritis is associated with chronic pain and contributes to multiple years lived with disability. Chronic knee pain varies between patients due to the influence of multiple psychosocial risk (pain catastrophizing, depression) and resilience (optimism) factors. In this longitudinal study, we used mechanism-based clinical phenotypes to classify patients with knee pain into predominant nociceptive, neuropathic, or nociplastic pain groups, or mixed neuropathic/nociplastic pain groups, and to investigate their respective clinical and psychosocial profiles at baseline and 2 years later. Community-dwelling adults with knee osteoarthritis (n=177) completed questionnaires, function performance, and neuroimaging. Cluster analysis was used to identify pain profiles, and analysis of covariance was conducted to assess differences across pain groups in clinical pain and disability, and psychosocial risk and resilience outcome variables. Additionally, resting-state fMRI analyses were conducted to characterize whole-brain intrinsic connectivity differences between the pain groups. Results revealed significant group differences in psychosocial risk [catastrophizing (F = 12.2, p < 0.001), depression (F = 9.74, p < 0.001)] and resilience [optimism (F = 1.97, p = 0.120)] factors, clinical pain [(F = 18.91, p < 0.001)], disability [(F = 16.62, p < 0.001)], and functional performance [(F = 2.24, p = 0.086)], controlling for sociodemographic covariates. Indeed, the mixed neuropathic/nociplastic pain group showed the poorest outcomes. Two years later, there were group differences in multiple measures, including psychosocial risk [catastrophizing (F = 12.66, p < 0.001), depression (F = 2.76, p = 0.045)], clinical pain [(F = 6.46, p < 0.001)] and disability [(F = 6.28, p < 0.001)], and movement-evoked pain [(F = 7.93, p < 0.001)]. The neuropathic group showed reduced brain connectivity in regions associated with the dorsal attention and visual networks, compared with the nociceptive group. In contrast, we observed differences in the default mode and frontoparietal networks between the neuropathic/nociplastic and nociceptive groups. Together, these findings demonstrate that mechanism-based pain profiles may be associated with distinctive clinical and psychosocial risk and resilience factors that may differentiate these pain groups. These clinical, behavioral, and neurobiological profiles may have clinical utility and can be used to optimize a biopsychosocial framework for assessment, diagnosis, and treatment of individuals with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis. Future research should investigate the mixed pain groups.

abstract: Circadian clocks regulate daily behaviors like sleep and locomotion, but little is known about how the primary motor cortex (M1) participates in circadian regulation of motor behaviors. To determine if neuronal activity in M1 changes with time of day, we used in vivo fiber photometry to record cell-type-specific calcium fluorescence in layer 5 (L5) of M1 neurons from freely moving C57 mice. We measured calcium events (e.g. peak heights and integrated intensity) for 10 min every hour over multiple days in mice injected with AAV8 Syn-GCaMP8m and implanted with a fiber optic in L5. M1 neurons showed daily rhythms (Metacycle, p<0.001) in calcium events under a 7am:7pm light:dark cycle, peaking in the early night (ZT 14.7 ± SEM, n=7 mice; Rayleigh test, P<0.0001). These rhythms persisted in constant darkness with a period of 23.8 h ± SEM, n=7 mice). In contrast, control mice injected with AAV8 Syn-EGFP in L5 did not show daily rhythms in fluorescence. We next test if M1 neurons require the core circadian clock gene, Bmal1, to control daily rhythms in motor behavior and M1 Ca2+. We injected AAV8 Syn-Cre tdTomato or Syn-m-cherry bilaterally into M1 of Bmal1fl/fl mice and found that, compared to controls, ablation of Bmal1 in M1 neurons reduced the amplitude and anticipation of daily rhythms in Ca2+ (t-test, p<0.05) and locomotion (t-test, p<0.01). We conclude that a circadian clock in M1 neurons entrains to local time and promotes daily increases in neuronal activity and rest-wake behavior.

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) describes the processes by which agents or organisms learn, through trial and error, to predict and take actions that maximize cumulative reward. Different aspects of RL are thought to be dependent on functionally heterogenous striatal circuits. Mounting evidence show that astrocytes can actively regulate neuronal function in these circuits. They can modulate up to hundreds of thousands of synapses per cell through astrocytic calcium dynamics (ACD) that can occur on a spectrum of spatiotemporal scales. In theory, astrocytes could uniquely contribute to neuronal circuits by helping to address a key function required for cognitive operations: adaptively regulating variability within local circuits to produce stable representations to guide behavior. However, whether and how astrocytes support specific behavioral computations in RL-guided behavior across striatum is still poorly understood. To start to assess this question, we attenuated astrocyte calcium activity across different subregions of striatum while animals performed a RL-dependent probabilistic reversal task. This computationally tractable task allowed us to model the effects of ACD attenuation within a normative learning framework. We found that attenuation of ACD in DMS and DLS had relatively little impact on key reinforcement learning parameters, such as on learning rate and inverse temperature (decision noisiness). In contrast, VS ACD attenuation decreased inverse temperature (increasing decision noisiness) and impaired reward-guided choice performance, specifically by reducing win-stay behavior. Using fiber photometry to monitor ACD during RL revealed that VS ACD reflected model inferred reward prediction errors (RPEs), for many seconds after the outcome, until the start of the next trial. We built a biologically constrained circuit model of neuron-astrocyte interactions to assess how astrocyte encoding of RPE learning signals could support RL-guided decision-making. In both photometry-obtained ACD and in our circuit model, trial-by-trial ACD fluctuations predicted trial-by-trial choice variability, particularly in win-stay behavior. In-silico experiments suggested that choice performance and win-stay behavior could be mediated by astrocytes averaging and sharing dopaminergic RPE inputs across MSN populations. These findings highlight a specific role of ACD in RL through the regulation of decision noisiness and win-stay stability, and they generate novel hypotheses for how astrocytes modulate the circuits underlying value-based decision-making and cognition.

abstract: Stroke is the leading cause of chronic disability in the United States, and advancing age is associated with worse recovery. Yet relatively little is known about how aging influences the repair and reorganization of neural circuits and large-scale cortical networks after stroke. We used wide-field calcium imaging to compare cortical network dynamics and behavioral recovery after focal photothrombotic stroke in forepaw somatosensory cortex in young (3-month-old) and aged (18-month-old) Thy1-GCaMP6f mice. Both young and aged mice developed significant somatomotor deficits after stroke, but only young mice exhibited substantial behavioral recovery despite similar infarct volumes across groups. While young and aged mice showed differences in baseline forepaw-evoked response amplitudes and their trajectories after stroke, the temporal dynamics of these circuits were comparable between young and aged mice both before and after stroke, suggesting a degree of resilience of local neuronal circuits. Neuronal network dynamics proved to be a more sensitive measure of age- and stroke-related degradation. Young mice demonstrated more coordinated neuronal network dynamics at baseline, as measured by hemispheric stimulus-locked fidelity, bilateral coherence, and cortical entrainment, that were significantly disrupted after stroke and did not recover after 7 weeks; aged mice exhibited disorganized network dynamics at baseline and no significant changes after stroke. Reductions in the spatial extent of cortical entrainment between baseline and 1-week post-stroke predicted long-term behavioral recovery across animals and groups. Finally, only young mice showed significant recovery of somatosensory and somatomotor functional connectivity by 7 weeks after stroke. These results suggest similarities in neuronal network degradation caused by aging and stroke and highlight the vulnerability of neuronal networks, relative to local neuronal circuits, in both processes. Our findings also indicate a potential network-level basis for chronic deficits in stroke survivors.

abstract: Early cortical surface area hyperexpansion from 6-12 months has been observed in infants who later develop autism within the Infant Brain Imaging Study (IBIS), the largest longitudinal study of infants (>250 participants) at high familial likelihood for autism. While this research has provided key insights into early brain development, the cellular and molecular mechanisms driving this overgrowth remain unknown. To address this, our lab generated iPSCs from 115 IBIS participants: high-likelihood individuals who developed ASD (HL+), high-likelihood who did not (HL-), and low-likelihood who did not (LL-): all with longitudinal neuroimaging (6-24 months), behavioral assessments, and genotyping. We hypothesize ASD cortical overgrowth is driven by increased proliferative neural progenitor cells making symmetric cell fate decisions prenatally. To test this, we generated human cortical organoids (hCOs) differentiated to 84 days, completing differentiation for 108/115 participants. Organoid cross-sectional area correlated with in vivo cortical surface area growth in the same individual across multiple timepoints: for example, organoid growth from day 18 to 35 correlated with MRI-measured growth from 12 to 24 months (Pearson, r=0.502, p< 0.05, FDR corrected). Male derived organoids were significantly larger than female derived organoids from D18 (p<0.05) to D84 (p<0.001), mirroring known in vivo sex differences in cortical surface area, validating fidelity of cortical organoids as a model of inter-individual variation. Single cell RNA sequencing across 108 participants at day 14 and 84 yielded 1.5M high quality cells: the largest iPSC derived organoid scRNA seq dataset in an autism cohort. Annotations revealed expected cortical progenitor and neuronal subtypes, with proportions shifting from progenitor dominated at day 14 to neuron rich at day 84. Cell type composition was more correlated within replicates of the same participant than across participants (p=0.005 at D14; p<0.001 at D84), suggesting genetic background primarily drives cell type proportions. For lineage tracing, we introduced STICR (single cell RNA seq compatible lineage tracer with ~35 million unique barcodes) into hCOs from 31 donors. Across these experiments, 323K cells were sequenced, including 120K barcode positive cells, enabling tests of donor specific clonal expansion and radial unit organization. By combining organoid models, single cell RNA sequencing, lineage tracing, and clinical data, we aim to better understand ASD related brain development mechanisms in a deeply phenotyped iPSC population.

abstract:
Human brain organoids provide unique opportunities for studying early aspects of human neurodevelopment and disease mechanisms, but high inter-organoid variability and fragmented analytical practices limit their translational use and cross-study validation. We developed Organoid Integrated Open Network (ORION), an open‑source computational framework that captures and organizes all data and metadata for brain organoid generation and characterization from multi-electrode array (MEA) and patch-clamp recordings. We used ORION to characterize neuronal activity in telencephalic brain organoids with and without glioblastoma (GBM) across continuous 3-week recordings using an incubator-integrated MEA platform. We recorded from 16 control organoids and 8 GBM-organoid co-cultures across multiple stem cell and GBM lines. ORION integrates community tools to process electrical recordings and extract functional measurements for single-unit activity, functional connectivity, spectral decomposition, and phase-amplitude coupling (Fig. 1a).
ORION‑extracted measurements were analyzed using an AI‑assisted framework that prioritizes and interprets MEA metrics based on prior electrophysiology literature. From this analysis, we observed reduced tonic spiking in the presence of GBM, evident from prolonged inter-spike intervals (ISIs), consistent with “tumor‑core activity” described in non‑proliferating tumor regions in patients and mice (Fig. 1b). To validate the chosen metrics, we used a linear mixed effects model that quantifies contributions of GBM status, stem cell lineage, and inter‑organoid and inter‑electrode variability to the observed variance (Fig. 1c). ORION provides a scalable, fully documented ecosystem that links organoid generation metadata with automated AI-assisted electrophysiology analysis and robust metric validation, accelerating the use of brain organoids as models for studying neural development and disease.

abstract: Locus ceruleus (LC)-derived norepinephrine (NE) drives network and behavioral adaptations to environmental saliencies by reconfiguring circuit functional connectivity, but the underlying synapse-level mechanisms are elusive. In this work, we showed that NE remodeling of synaptic function is completely independent from its binding on neuronal receptors. Instead, astrocytic α1a adrenergic receptors (α1a-AR) and astrocyte calcium dynamics fully gate the effect of NE on synapses. Additionally, we found that NE suppression of synaptic strength results from an adenosine 5′-triphosphate (ATP)-derived and A1 adenosine receptor-mediated control of presynaptic efficacy. These findings suggest that astrocytes are a core component of neuromodulatory systems and the circuit effector through which NE produces network and behavioral adaptations

abstract: Structural plasticity of dendritic spines in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) is critical for learning from aversive experiences. Activation of NMDA receptors (NMDARs) triggers Ca2+-dependent signaling cascades that regulate actin cytoskeletal remodeling through Rho family GTPases, thereby driving postsynaptic structural changes that support learning. Here, we investigated phosphorylation events downstream of NMDAR activation that link Ca2+ signaling to synaptic plasticity and aversive learning. Large-scale phosphoproteomic analysis of mouse striatal slices containing the NAc identified 194 proteins whose phosphorylation was increased following NMDAR activation, including the RhoA regulators ARHGEF2 and ARHGAP21. CaMKII-mediated phosphorylation of ARHGEF2 enhanced its Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor activity, resulting in activation of RhoA and its downstream effector, Rho-associated protein kinase (Rho-kinase/ROCK). Reduced ROCK function in accumbal dopamine D2 receptor-expressing medium spiny neurons (D2R-MSNs) impaired dendritic spine structural plasticity, long-term potentiation (LTP), and aversive learning. To identify downstream effectors of ROCK, phosphoproteomic analysis identified 221 putative ROCK substrates, including the postsynaptic scaffold protein SHANK3. ROCK-dependent phosphorylation of SHANK3 in the NAc was required for dendritic spine growth and aversive learning. In a schizophrenia-like mouse model induced by repeated NMDAR antagonist administration, mice exhibited impaired aversive learning and reduced aversive stimulus-evoked Ca2+ transients in NAc D2R-MSNs. Consistent with these deficits, activation of the CaMKII-RhoA-ROCK signaling pathway was attenuated. Collectively, these findings identify an NMDAR-initiated phosphorylation cascade—CaMKII-ARHGEF2-RhoA-ROCK-SHANK3—that links Ca2+ influx to structural and functional postsynaptic plasticity in D2R-MSNs and supports aversive learning. Impairment of this pathway may contribute to aversive-learning deficits associated with NMDAR hypofunction.

abstract: The periaqueductal gray (PAG) coordinates defensive and pain-related responses through functionally distinct columnar populations. Within the ventrolateral PAG (vlPAG), mu opioid receptor (MOR) activation has been implicated in passive defensive behaviors and analgesia. However, it remains unclear how vlPAG MOR neurons respond across distinct threat modalities, whether projection-defined MOR populations contribute to defensive behaviors, and how endogenous opioid signaling is engaged across different threat states. Here, we combined in vivo calcium imaging, projection-specific circuit manipulations, and real-time enkephalin detection to characterize threat responsivity and endogenous opioid dynamics in adult mice of both sexes. Miniscope calcium imaging revealed robust, overlapping encoding across diverse innate and learned threat types. The threat-responsive ensembles showed substantial overlap with MOR-expressing neurons, which project to forebrain and hindbrain regions linked to pain, stress, and motivational processing. We parsed the vlPAG MOR neurons into transcriptionally-, projection-, and noxious activity-defined clusters using spatial transcriptomics. This analysis uncovered a highly activated posterior vlPAG MOR-expressing cluster projecting to the medial thalamus. To discern the behavioral function of this pathway, we used an intersectional viral approach. Chemogenetic inhibition of the vlPAG-thalamus pathway significantly reduced behavioral responses to multiple noxious threats, demonstrating a causal role in nociceptive responding. To examine endogenous opioid dynamics associated with vlPAG threat processing, we used the genetically-encoded enkephalin sensor δLight to monitor extracellular enkephalin signaling onto vlPAG MOR neurons. Acute noxious stimulation was associated with decreased enkephalin release, whereas prolonged nociceptive states were associated with increased enkephalin release, revealing distinct patterns of endogenous opioid engagement across noxious threat conditions. We next examined enkephalin dynamics during a conditioned safety assay, in which mice learned to associate a context with reduced noxious threat. Conditioning reduced affective-motivational responses by nearly a third. This effect was accompanied by increased enkephalin release relative to unconditioned controls. Together, these findings identify a projection-defined vlPAG MOR circuit that contributes to behavioral responses to noxious threat and demonstrate that endogenous enkephalin signaling dynamically tunes acute, prolonged, and learned threat states.

abstract: Preschool- and elementary-aged children spend significantly more time with peers than infants and toddlers, making this a salient period to study early neural responses to social feedback. The present study aimed to measure differences in children’s neural activity (i.e., EEG frequency bands) to peer acceptance versus rejection and determine whether age and sex were associated with responsivity. Children aged 4 to 7 years old (n=173; Mean age (SD) = 6.26 (1.06) years) completed the playdate task and received feedback about whether peers wanted to play with them (acceptance) versus not play with them (rejection), with trials randomized across the task. Time frequency analyses isolated and averaged 5000ms windows during accept and reject conditions at electrode Fz. T-statistic topographic maps were created to identify and extract data from regions of interest (5ms of significant condition differences, recorded at 1000Hz sampling rate) and multitaper phase locking was used. Across children, responsivity differences to condition were observed in gamma and late alpha-beta frequency bands (greater responsivity to acceptance; p’s < .02) as well as in delta-theta, delta, theta, and early alpha-beta frequency bands (greater responsivity to rejection; p’s < .003). In moderator analyses, older children showed greater responsivity in alpha-beta, delta-theta, and late alpha-beta frequency bands to both types of feedback (p’s < .001). Older children also had greater responsivity in delta and theta bands and greater differences based on feedback type (with larger response to rejection; p’s < .001). When examining sex moderations, girls had greater overall delta, theta, and delta-theta responsivity than boys across both conditions (p’s < .02). Compared to boys who had similar responsivity across conditions in early alpha-beta bands, girls had much greater responsivity to rejection than acceptance (p = 0.02). Conversely, boys had a greater responsivity difference in gamma frequency bands, with a larger response to acceptance, compared to girls (p = 0.03). Taken together, findings indicate that, responsivity to rejection is greater at most frequency bands compared with acceptance, and there are age- and sex-related differences, with older children and girls exhibiting greater responsivity to feedback. Findings indicate that neural response peer rejection is increasingly salient in girls and as children enter school-age in early childhood. Future work should examine social functioning and psychiatric predictors of responsivity differences.

abstract: Aberrant cytoplasmic accumulation of TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is a pathological hallmark of most amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases. Although overexpressing human TDP-43 with a deleted nuclear localization signal (hTDP-43ΔNLS) in mice recapitulates the cytoplasmic mislocalization observed in ALS, existing models generally rely on broad or non-selective expression in all types of neurons or cells, limiting their ability to appreciate cell-autonomous effects. We developed a method to selectively overexpress spinal motor neuron-specific mislocalization of hTDP-43 into cytoplasm, by intrathecally injecting a Cre-dependent pAAV-PHP.eB-CAG-DIO-hTDP-43ΔNLS virus into 4-week-old B6;129S6-Chattm2(cre)Lowl/J transgenic mice. CHAT-dependent hTDP-43ΔNLS transgenic mice exhibited robust hindlimb clasping as early as 2 weeks post-injection (2wpi), indicating early motor dysfunction. Consistent with this phenotype, the mice showed ALS-like behavioral deficits, including reduced grip strength and impaired performance in rotarod and wire hang tests at 4wpi. Kinematic gait analysis is capable of detecting subtle locomotor abnormalities with high precision but has been rarely used in ALS studies. We optimized this approach for ALS models, enabling detailed characterization of multiple aspects of locomotor dysfunction in our model. Hindlimb kinematic analysis further confirmed locomotor impairment, revealing reduced hindlimb joint heights, shortened stride length, and impaired hindlimb support. These motor deficits were supported by marked peripheral neuromuscular pathology, as shown by sciatic nerves axonal loss and degeneration, muscle atrophy, reduced compound muscle action potential amplitudes (CMAP), and pronounced neuromuscular junction (NMJ) denervation and structural disruption. Collectively, we established a novel spinal motor neuron-restricted hTDP-43ΔNLS mouse model that recapitulates key behavioral and pathological features of ALS. This model provides a valuable platform for investigating cell-autonomous mechanisms and potential therapeutic targets.

abstract: There are sex-based differences in the susceptibility to chronic pain and autoimmune diseases, with those assigned female at birth often showing the highest burden. In mice, the maintenance of chronic pain is dependent on sex hormone levels and specific leukocyte populations, with males utilizing microglia and females utilizing T cells. Notably, T cells are key contributors to many autoimmune conditions, which are typically more prevalent in females. This biological, sex-based difference in immune cell usage is often equated to a socially constructed, sex-based difference but may be more appropriately characterized as a result of predominant circulating hormones. However, past studies have either enrolled only cisgender adults and/or excluded those on exogenous hormones. Given the increased prevalence of hormone use across multiple populations and the impact of sex hormones on immune cells populations, it is important to assess these associations in healthy adults with known levels of circulating endogenous and/or exogenous hormones. The present study aimed to investigate the role of sex hormones on immune cell populations in healthy adults. Eligible participants (N= 119) included cisgender men (n= 29) and women (n= 34), transgender men (n= 14) and women (n= 15), and non-binary individuals (assigned female at birth, n= 13; assigned male at birth, n= 11) between the ages of 18-65 who reported no chronic pain or autoimmune conditions. After a blood draw, plasma was used to assess leukocyte populations (flow cytometry) and sex hormone levels (multiplex assays). Preliminary data analyses showed that testosterone levels were associated with the frequency of NK cells and CD3+, CD4+, activated CD4+, activated CD8+ cells, and regulatory T cells, such that those with lower testosterone levels had higher frequencies of all T cell types and lower frequencies of NK cells. Sex assigned at birth (SAB; male/female) was associated with testosterone levels and regulatory T cell frequency, but it was not associated with other immune cell population levels. However, gender (man/woman) was associated with testosterone levels as well as frequency of CD3+ and CD4+ T cells, as well as NK cells. These preliminary findings suggest that the previously observed sex differences in chronic pain and autoimmune conditions may be due to circulating hormone levels and are more reflective of gender (whether cisgender or transgender) than SAB. Together, these data suggest that the introduction of exogenous hormones (e.g., hormone replacement therapies, testosterone use in aging men, etc.) may impact immunological systems and affect risk for chronic pain and autoimmune conditions.

abstract: The advent of high-density silicon microelectrodes in the field of human single-unit neurophysiology has expanded our ability to map the cortical surface during neurosurgical procedures. However, despite both clinical and scientific interest in performing such recordings deeper in the brain, the required length and risk of electrode fracture make such deeper recordings impossible with current technology. Thus, microelectrode recordings in the basal ganglia during Deep-Brain Stimulation (DBS) surgery are, to this day, performed one depth at a time using a small number of single channel microelectrodes. Here, we demonstrate that large-scale, high-density extracellular recordings are achievable in the human basal ganglia using a novel 128-channel microelectrode array fabricated on a stainless-steel substrate, thus obviating the risk of electrode fracture and allowing for the development of very long electrodes that can reach the human basal ganglia. Microelectrodes on this array are spread over 3.175mm with a vertical pitch of 50μm and horizontal pitch of 43.3μm, allowing for dense recording of local field potentials and observation of the same action potential waveform across multiple channels. We use this information to perform robust spike sorting using state of the art motion-artifact correction and spike sorting techniques. Using this microelectrode array, we reliably perform simultaneous recording from ~100 neurons in the subthalamic nucleus (STN) of PD patients undergoing DBS surgery. We perform these recordings during resting wakefulness and characterize neuronal β-oscillatory dynamics as well as neuronal entrainment and waveform modulation throughout the cardiac cycle. Furthermore, we perform recordings while patients are engaged in a Stop Signal task and demonstrate that core findings from previous work, which required pooling data across many subjects, can be recapitulated in individual patients. Furthermore, we show that the geometry of encoded task variables can be studied with single-session and single-trial resolution. Indeed, the number of neurons required to match state-of-the-art publications, whose data were collected over the course of several years, can be attained in a single recording session with our approach. Our work heralds the beginning of a significant acceleration in the science dedicated to the mapping of deep structures within the human brain, and provides a novel approach through which our understanding and treatment of neurological disease can be revolutionized.

abstract: Stroke is a leading cause of disability worldwide, with many patients suffering from chronic motor impairment. However, there is significant heterogeneity in the structural and functional damage observed following a stroke. Despite most patients suffering chronic motor impairments having predominately subcortical damage, most preclinical research focuses on cortical strokes, potentially biasing pre-clinical translatability. To address this challenge, we used a within-subject photothrombotic stroke model to determine whether recovery of skilled reaching kinematics differs following a cortical (M1-FL) or subcortical (internal capsule) lesion in rodents. Long-Evans rats (n = 8) were trained on a skilled pellet retrieval task. Following training, rodents were implanted with a chronic fiber-optic cannula directly above M1-FL (n=3) or with an optoelectric cannula implanted within the internal capsule (n=5). After implantation, rodents performed at least five 30-minute baseline sessions with 30-50 reach trials per session over 2-3-weeks. At 3 weeks rats underwent rose Bengal photothrombosis under isoflourane anesthesia. Post-lesion rodents performed three sessions in the first week and then two sessions per week for weeks 2-8. Offline, reach and grasp events were manually scored, and the 2D positions of the nose and forelimb joints were tracked across all videos with DeepLabCut. The capsular lesion group showed a drastic reduction in normalized task success, relative to the cortical group (p < 0.001). Following capsular infarcts, rodents did not recover greater than 5% of pre-lesion success, so all kinematic differences were assessed on failed attempts. The cortical group recovered success to ~65% of pre-lesion levels at about 3 weeks post-lesion. Capsular rodents had a declined mean wrist speed and increased tortuosity of the wrist path relative to pre-lesion levels (dz = 1.90, dz = -2.56). Cortical rodents showed initial decline in speed and path smoothness but recovered the baseline movement trajectories at ~3 weeks. Our results indicate that after different lesions rodents recover separate motor profiles for a skilled reaching task. This is also the first demonstration of utilizing a chronically implanted optoelectric probe to lesion the internal capsule. Future studies will collect bilateral electrophysiological data to assess within-subjects alterations in task-related neural activity and motor performance following a focal infarct and during recovery. Furthermore, utilizing 3D pose-estimation will enable greater inferences on the relative contributions of distal and proximal motor control on recovered behavior.

abstract: A core tenet of systems neuroscience is that the electrical ‘spiking’ activity of individual neurons gives rise to cognition and behavior. Recent work has shown that both transcriptomic identity of a neuron and its brain region are decodable from features of single-neuron spike timing, which proves that spiking activity encodes broad variables related to neurobiology beyond the single neuron’s contribution. However, single-neuron encoding has not been investigated in relation to animal behavior. Here, we asked whether an animal’s arousal state is also decodable from individual neuron spiking, and whether this information is impaired by disease. We analyzed a dataset of multi-region, electrophysiological recordings of single-unit activity from freely-behaving mice that were split into two cohorts: wild-type (N=9) and APP/PS1 (N=8), a model of Alzheimer’s Disease. We trained machine learning classifiers on neural activity throughout many naturally-occurring sleep-wake cycles. With several classification approaches, we found that arousal state is significantly decodable from both selected features of the spiking activity of individual neurons and the distributions of their inter-spike intervals, a capacity which is significantly reduced by disease progression. We also found varied disease effects by brain region, with predictive capacity more impaired in selectively-vulnerable regions associated with cognitive functioning, compared to regions typically unaffected by Alzheimer’s progression such as the visual cortex. This implies a connection between region functionality and sleep state classifiability from individual neurons. This work adds to a growing hypothesis that patterns of neural spiking contain rich, multiplexed information about cellular identity and behavioral state, and suggests that stable encoding of this information could be crucial for healthy brain function.

abstract: Glioblastomas (GBM) conventionally are viewed as disrupting brain function. However, emerging evidence shows that glioma cells can form activity-dependent synaptic connections with neurons. We hypothesized that resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) can identify functionally distinct tumor subregions which interact with canonical resting-state networks (RSNs). We analyzed preoperative rs-fMRI from 190 patients with IDH-wildtype GBM and 347 healthy controls. Voxelwise blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) time series were extracted from contrast-enhancing tumor regions, reduced using principal component analysis, and clustered using fuzzy c-means clustering. Cluster-average time series were correlated with seven canonical RSNs and compared with anatomically matched regions in healthy subjects. Fifty-two of 190 tumors (27.4%) exhibited multiple spatially coherent functional clusters. In many cases (29/52 (55.8%) multi-cluster tumors; 14/138 (10.1%) single-cluster tumors), these functional connections were stronger than those in a reference cohort. Elevated RSN coupling was strongly associated with multi-cluster status after adjustment for age, sex, and tumor size (OR=14.11, 95% CI 6.05-32.93, p=9.1×10⁻¹⁰). Multi-cluster tumors demonstrated increased seizure prevalence (adjusted OR=3.33, 95% CI 1.53-7.23, p=0.00245) and longer survival than single-cluster tumors (median survival 506 vs. 367 days; adjusted RMST difference +95.7 days, p=0.018). These findings identify a subset of GBMs characterized by functional subregions and selective coupling to distributed brain networks, suggesting a potential prognostic biomarker based on rs-fMRI.

abstract: The E4 allele of the APOE gene, APOE4, is the major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease (AD), compared to APOE3 that carries lower risk. Early blood-brain barrier (BBB) breakdown occurs in AD and is thought to contribute to cognitive impairment. APOE4 exerts substantial cerebrovascular toxicity including BBB breakdown both in humans and in APOE transgenic models, which we previously showed precedes cognitive impairment and synaptic deficits.Here, we investigated neurodegenerative and BBB changes in 9.5-month-old APOE3 and APOE4 knock-in floxed (F) mice, i.e., E3F and E4F, alone and crossed with a mouse model of tauopathy (Tau P301S). We observed neurodegenerative changes at 9.5-months, with reduced hippocampal neuronal density in E4F compared to E3F mice and further degeneration in mice with tauopathy, with E4F; P301S mice exhibiting the greatest loss of neuronal density. Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry proteomic and phosphoproteomic analysis of post-synaptic density (PSD) fractions isolated from these mice indicated substantial synaptic protein loss and dysregulation of synaptic signaling networks. The synaptic phenotypes followed a similar pattern with a synergic increase in the severity with E4F; P301S mice most affected. Immunostaining for blood-derived fibrinogen revealed increasing BBB leakage in E4F compared to E3F mice, which was further exacerbated by tauopathy, with the most severe BBB leakage observed in the E4F; P301S mice.Together this data suggests that neurodegenerative changes and BBB breakdown are more severe in APOE4 compared to APOE3 mice, and APOE4 expression combined with tau pathology co-act to increase the severity of neurodegenerative and BBB pathology.

abstract: Often characterized by severe impairments in communication, Rett Syndrome (RTT) results from mutations in the gene encoding for methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2). Yet the cortical circuit disruptions underlying these impairments remain unclear. Given the Auditory Cortex's (ACx) critical function in decoding behaviorally relevant acoustic signals, we asked how loss of MeCP2 alters sound-evoked activity and local excitatory connectivity. Using hemizygous male MeCP2 knockout mice (MeCP2-KO), we combined sound stimulation with Fos immunolabeling and whole-brain clearing to map neuronal activation across sound categories. Compared to wild-type mice, MeCP2-KO mice showed disrupted hemispheric organization of sound-evoked activity in the ACx, with a prominent loss of deep-layer (L4-6) recruitment in the left ACx. Consistent with this phenotype, MeCP2-KO mice also showed abnormal processing of social vocalizations in behavioral assays. To identify circuit mechanisms underlying these abnormalities, we used laser scanning photostimulation with glutamate uncaging to map excitatory synaptic connectivity. We first focused on L3, a major site of spectral integration, and found that total excitatory input to L3 was reduced in the left ACx of MeCP2-KO mice. Across all cortical layers, this target-layer deficit was matched by a source-layer abnormality with reduced excitatory output from L4-6 in the left ACx. The stronger expression of both deficits in the left ACx suggests that MeCP2 loss disrupts deep-layer cortical output and normal auditory cortical specialization. Preliminary developmental results further suggest that these abnormalities emerge in the context of disrupted maturation of inhibitory and extracellular matrix-associated programs during postnatal circuit refinement. Together, these findings identify a candidate cortical circuit basis for communication deficits in RTT: a failure of deep-to-superficial circuit assembly, marked by weak deep-layer output and altered maturation of superficial target circuitry.

abstract: Transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS), when paired with physical therapy, has been shown to improve motor outcomes in people with spinal cord injury (SCI), even in the chronic stage of injury. However, the therapeutic effects of tSCS vary widely across individuals and may depend on the tuning of stimulation parameters, with current approaches remaining poorly optimized. The amplitude at which stimulation is administered is inconsistent across studies, and is typically based on either participant tolerance, paresthesia, or threshold amplitudes for evoked muscle responses. Therefore, the effect of SCS amplitude on motor facilitation for both single-joint and multi-joint coordinated movement remains poorly understood. In this study, we examine the effect of tSCS amplitude on motor facilitation during single-joint isometric movement and multi-joint coordinated movement during cycling. Participants with incomplete (ASIA B-D) SCI completed isometric maximum voluntary contractions (MVCs) of the ankle, knee, and hip joints with and without tSCS at different tSCS amplitudes over five sessions. Magnitude of MVCs and EMG activation were used as primary outcome measures to determine the motor-enabling effect of tSCS. During a separate session, participants completed active (semi-assisted) and passive cycling with and without tSCS. To date, two participants have completed the protocol. Both participants exhibited a training effect, as movements got stronger over sessions. For one participant, there appeared to be a learning period in which they adapted to using tSCS for movement, and MVC amplitude was enhanced by tSCS only during sessions 3-5. EMG activation was enhanced at tSCS amplitudes between 70-100% of motor threshold, although higher stimulation amplitudes could cause co-contraction and decrease net torque output, or even cause torque generation in the opposite direction. Subthreshold tSCS at 35-66% of the motor threshold improved cycling movement smoothness compared to the no-stimulation condition. However, tSCS at 100% of motor threshold reduced this improvement due to widespread activation of leg muscles. Data collection for additional participants and further data analysis are ongoing and will be presented at the conference together with these results.

abstract: Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) has demonstrated significant potential for improving motor function following spinal cord injury (SCI). While transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) offers a noninvasive means to activate leg muscles below the injury, neural recruitment suffers from low selectivity due to the long distance between the stimulation site and the targeted spinal neural structures. Consequently, the stimulation parameters required to achieve targeted motor activation with tSCS remain poorly understood. The focus of this study is to investigate how stimulation frequency modulates flexor- and extensor-related motor output during voluntary movement. We hypothesize that lower stimulation frequencies preferentially engage monosynaptic pathways, facilitating extensor-dominant motor output, whereas higher frequencies promote greater involvement of polysynaptic circuitry through temporal summation, enhancing flexor-dominant activation. To test this hypothesis, individuals with SCI perform maximum voluntary contractions (MVCs) of the ankle, knee, and hip joints during flexion and extension isometric tasks while receiving continuous tSCS at varying stimulation frequencies. Peak torque from MVCs at each joint is used as the primary outcome measure for motor facilitation. Frequency-dependent changes in torque and evoked responses via EMG are used to evaluate both the overall motor-enabling effects of stimulation and the potential preferential recruitment of flexor or extensor motor pools. If successful, results from this study could lead to selective activation of flexor vs extensor muscles by controlling tSCS frequency depending on movement phase, thus improving coordinated movement in people with SCI.

abstract: Transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) is a non-invasive approach that can immediately facilitate motor function after spinal cord injury (SCI). However, the magnitude of this immediate prosthetic effect and the neural mechanisms that enable it remain poorly understood. To characterize the motor-enabling effect of tSCS, we compared peak torque during isometric contractions performed with and without 30-Hz tSCS over the T11/T12 vertebral segments. Ten participants with chronic SCI (AIS C-D; injury levels between C3-L1; >1-year post-injury) performed five maximum voluntary contractions during hip, knee, and ankle flexion and extension, both with and without tSCS. Stimulation amplitude was set to either the target muscle's motor threshold or the maximum tolerable amplitude. Per-condition linear mixed models (peak torque ~ stimulation, random intercept per participant) revealed that tSCS significantly increased peak torque for hip extension (left +3.03 Nm, 95% CI [1.11, 4.96], p = 0.006; right +2.83 Nm, [0.74, 4.91], p = 0.016), ankle plantarflexion (left +1.43 Nm, [0.70, 2.17], p < 0.001), and ankle dorsiflexion (left +1.20 Nm, [0.67, 1.74], p < 0.001; right +0.91 Nm, [0.29, 1.53], p = 0.010), and significantly decreased it for right hip flexion (−2.96 Nm, [−4.57, −1.35], p = 0.001; Benjamini-Hochberg corrected across 12 conditions). Knee torque did not change significantly in any condition (all p ≥ 0.10). A separate joint × direction mixed model revealed that tSCS facilitated extension over flexion at the hip (+4.17 Nm, [1.42, 6.92], p = 0.003) but not at the knee (+1.40 Nm, [−1.35, 4.15], p = 0.32) or ankle (−0.19 Nm, [−2.94, 2.56], p = 0.89). Extension facilitation was also significantly higher at the hip than at the ankle joint (4.36 Nm, [0.47, 8.25], p = 0.028). Ankle muscles typically required higher stimulation amplitudes to reach threshold. At these amplitudes, low-threshold proximal muscles may have been involuntarily activated, potentially interfering with participants’ volitional attempts. We further examined interactions between supraspinal, voluntary drive and tSCS by comparing the likelihood of tSCS enabling EMG burst-like activity versus stimulation-evoked responses during the active contraction periods. Further data collection and analysis are currently ongoing. Together, findings presented at the conference will aim to quantify torque increases that can be expected with tSCS and provide insights into whether tSCS-mediated motor facilitation reflects a generalized increase in spinal excitability of voluntary gating of stimulation pulses acting on afferent fibers within the posterior roots.

abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) causes a loss of motor and/or sensory functions. Transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) is a non-invasive method to activate dormant muscles below the injury and has shown functional improvements in chronic SCI when paired with activity-based training. However, how tSCS and activity-based training, alone and in combination, can modulate the excitability of corticospinal, reticulospinal, and spinal circuits, remains poorly understood. In a cross-over study design, we investigated short-term changes in neural excitability of the lower limbs as neurologically intact individuals (N = 18) completed 30-minute training sessions with: tSCS at the T11/T12 vertebral segments alone (tSCS), bilateral leg motor skill training (BoMi), tSCS combined with motor skill training (tSCS+BoMi), or tSCS plus high-intensity ankle resistance training (tSCS+resistance). Conditions were tested during separate sessions, and the order of testing was randomized. Corticospinal excitability was assessed by motor evoked potentials (MEPs) elicited with transcranial magnetic stimulation. Reticulospinal excitability was assessed by the reticulospinal gain during the StartReact task, a reduction in reaction time to a startling auditory cue. Spinal motoneuron excitability was analyzed via H-reflex/M-waves ratio (H/M) and F-wave amplitude/persistence of the right tibialis anterior using peripheral nerve stimulation. MEP amplitude (% Mmax) was modeled with a Gamma generalized linear mixed-effects model (log link). Motor skill training alone decreased MEP amplitude from pre to post (ratio = 1.13, p = 0.003), possibly reflecting the bilateral, multi-joint nature of the task. Adding tSCS to BoMi significantly altered the pre-to-post response relative to BoMi alone (pairwise interaction contrast, β = 0.18, p = 0.002), suggesting tSCS counteracted this reduction, when paired with BoMi. tSCS+resistance training significantly decreased MEP amplitude from pre to post (ratio = 1.24, p < 0.0001), and this pre-to-post change differed significantly from that of tSCS+BoMi (pairwise interaction contrast, β = 0.23, p < 0.0001). H/M ratio significantly increased after tSCS+BoMi (t(17) = 2.07, p = 0.05), but not during other conditions. The reticulospinal gain slightly decreased in extensors after tSCS+resistance (t(14) = -2.01, p = 0.06), although this change did not reach significance. This ongoing study clarifies short-term changes to neural excitability pathways related to training type, intensity, and stimulation.

abstract: Nucleoside analogues containing a bicyclo[3.1.0]hexane ring system (termed “methanocarba”) in place of ribose show promise as a privileged but not promiscuous structural class for interaction with diverse protein targets (Jacobson et al., 2017). Recently, certain (N)-methanocarba nucleosides were shown to also antagonize opioid receptors (ORs): δ- (DOR), κ-(KOR), and μ- (MOR), with moderate preference for KOR (Tosh et al., 2018). Expanding on this earlier report, and given the therapeutic value of KOR ligands in the treatment of pain and psychostimulant abuse, we employed a structure-guided design strategy informed by cryo-EM structural insights, coupled with semi-synthetic modification of a nucleoside compound to generate 10 novel methaocarba nucleosides for potential activity at the KOR. Pharmacological characterization began in vitro with functional cell-based assays (BRET imaging of Gi and beta-arrestins) for agonist or antagonist activity at all three OR. Analog MRS7299 displayed KOR antagonism, whereas MRS7414 displayed KOR-selective partial agonism. MD simulations and biophysical examination suggested the orientation and engagement with the KOR dictated the activity of the analogs. Behavioral studies in mice were conducted to evaluate antinociception (55oC warm-water tail-withdrawal model), confirming MRS7299 is a potent KOR antagonist with poor BBB-penetration. Testing also confirmed MRS7414 was a KOR-selective partial agonist, reaching only a ~50% antinociceptive response after administration of a 30 mg/kg s.c. dose. Tested at the estimated ED50 value of 41 mg/kg, s.c., MRS7414 increased respiration without sedative effects or conditioned place-aversion characteristic of KOR full agonists. However, pretreatment with MRS7414 prevented cocaine-conditioned place preference, consistent with the activity of KOR agonism. These data highlight the potential of structure-guided design to intentionally tune receptor agonist efficacy, identifying a promising potent KOR antagonist (MRS7299) and partial agonist (MRS7414) as potentially promising strategy to separate analgesia from opioid liabilities as well as new potential treatments for cocaine abuse.

abstract:
Opioid use disorder remains a major driver of morbidity and mortality, with withdrawal-associated aversive states contributing to relapse. The central amygdala (CeA) has been implicated in opioid withdrawal, but the specific subpopulations driving the somatic versus affective components remain poorly defined.
To map CeA activation during withdrawal, we precipitated withdrawal with naloxone in mice rendered opioid-dependent through repeated oxycodone administration. Whole-CeA cFos quantification showed broad activation across CeA subregions in withdrawn animals relative to naive and saline controls.
To gain genetic access to the withdrawal-activated population, we used Fos2A-iCreER (FosTRAP2) mice in combination with AAV-DIO-hM3D(Gq)-mCherry, capturing CeA neurons active during oxycodone withdrawal. Reactivation of these tagged neurons with clozapine N-oxide (CNO) in drug-naive animals produced a robust conditioned place aversion, indicating that this ensemble is sufficient to drive negative valence in the absence of the withdrawal state.
These data identify a withdrawal-activated CeA ensemble that is sufficient to encode the aversive component of opioid withdrawal, corroborating and extending recent work implicating the CeA in opioid withdrawal-induced negative affect.
