abstract: Opioid use disorder has been associated with maladaptive feeding. In mice, both acute and chronic morphine administration have been shown to reduce food intake and body weight. The GABAergic neurons of the lateral hypothalamus (LHVGAT) regulate feeding and appetitive behaviors and their activation is rewarding and triggers voracious intake of both palatable and non-palatable foods. However, it remains unclear how LHVGAT neurons modulate food intake and body weight during opioid dependence. Here, we used chemogenetics to test whether activation of LHVGAT neurons could overcome the anorexigenic effects of acute morphine administration. Concurrent activation of LHVGAT neurons with morphine administration significantly attenuated morphine-induced hypophagia, increased exploration of the food zone, and blunted morphine-induced hyperlocomotion. We next asked whether LHVGAT activation during morphine dependence could influence feeding behavior and body weight. Although activation increased food intake during dependence, it did not restore body weight, suggesting that LHVGAT-induced feeding does not mitigate morphine-associated weight loss. To determine whether altered thermogenesis contributed to this effect, we recorded core body temperature (CBT) using an intraperitoneal telemetry device before and after chemogenetic activation. Activation of LHVGAT neurons triggered a sustained increase in CBT, consistent with enhanced thermogenesis. We then assessed LHVGAT neuronal activity during acute morphine administration, chronic dependence, and naloxone-precipitated withdrawal using single-photon calcium imaging in awake mice. Acute morphine evoked dynamic changes in LHVGAT responses, including a subpopulation responsive to both saline and morphine. Across dependence and withdrawal, we recorded activity from 157 LHVGAT neurons and identified distinct subpopulations: 6% responded selectively to morphine, 17% responded selectively to naloxone, 10% exhibited opposing responses to morphine and naloxone, and 35% were co-modulated by both drugs. Finally, in situ hybridization revealed that approximately 40% of LHVGAT neurons express µ-opioid receptors (MORs). Together, our findings identify LHVGAT neurons as positive modulators of energy balance during morphine exposure and dependence and suggest that increased thermogenesis may limit their ability to restore body weight. Future studies will directly dissect the functional role of MOR-expressing LHVGAT neurons in modulating feeding.

abstract: Humans and many animals show an early-life tendency to explore and investigate novel stimuli. However, it remains unclear how this behavior develops across the lifespan and whether and how mothers contribute to it. We developed a longitudinal object-investigation paradigm in which mouse families (one dam and two offspring) were repeatedly exposed to either a novel or a familiar object during childhood (PD1–PD28). During development, they were tested either with the dam present (mother-present group) or in the dam's temporary absent (mother-absent group), allowing us to examine intrinsic behavioral responses to perceptual novelty and maternal influences. Once they became adults, offspring were again retested to determine how early-life experiences and maternal presence shaped their novelty-investigation behavior. To study exploratory object behavior, we concentrated on the animals’ object-directed approaches previously established to reflect object investigation: approaches with the tail relatively exposed to the object (tail-exposed) and approaches in which the tail was kept behind the body while the mice faced the object (tail-behind). Prior work has linked the tail-behind approach to rodent cautious investigation and risk assessment (Grant & Mackintosh, 1963; van der Poel, 1979; Kaesermann, 1986; Blanchard et al., 1991; Akiti et al., 2022). Our behavioral analyses show that in childhood, offspring approached novel objects relatively more cautiously than familiar objects. And this was observed even when analyzing the results for the mother-absent group suggesting that this behavior was not mother-dependent. Overall, maternal presence increased the proportion of tail-behind cautious approaches across all experimental conditions. Following maturation into adulthood, the mother-present group continued to exhibit relatively similar behavioral patterns to those that they exhibited in childhood, remaining more cautious toward novel objects. In contrast, the mother-absent group did not show consistent behavioral patterns across childhood and adulthood. And since the dams frequently retrieved their pups during experimental sessions, we investigated the impact of pup retrieval on offspring object-related behavior. We found that less cautious offspring became more cautious with more retrievals, suggesting that retrievals influenced offspring’s behavior well beyond the retrieval period itself. Together, these findings suggest that mothers play an active role in the long-term development of their offspring's exploratory behaviors across the lifespan.

abstract: Internally generated speech engages neural systems for speech planning and language, but word-level imagined speech remains difficult to study non-invasively because EEG signals are noisy. We tested whether the identity of an imagined word could be decoded from scalp EEG during a cued covert speech task. Participants performed imagined production of eight words (kick, open, throw, stop, clap, jump, yes, no) and a matched no-speech control condition while 28-channel EEG was recorded. Event-aligned EEG trials were preprocessed and used to train neural-network decoders to identify which word — or the control condition — had been imagined on each trial. Decoding accuracy approached 80% for the nine-way word/control classification, well above the 11.1% chance level. Channel- and time-resolved analysis indicated that the most informative recording sites and time windows differed across imagined words, suggesting partially distinct neural evidence for different speech targets. Together, these findings indicate that imagined speech generates reproducible, word-specific neural structure that can be captured non-invasively and decoded at the word level. The representational basis of this structure is the focus of ongoing analyses.

abstract: Resting-state functional MRI network topography can be used to study individual differences in functional organization that have been shown to covary with behavioral and clinical information (Bijsterbosch et al 2018; Lynch et al 2024; Wang et al 2015). Group and subject-level spatial topography maps are estimated via precision functional mapping (PFM) methods, but the consistency of network boundaries across PFM methods is unknown. We compared five PFM methods using the 6.1 release of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development cohort to investigate methodological and individual differences in network topography boundaries. After screening for motion and presence of three imaging sessions, we included N=3,050 subjects plus a held-out template group of N=100 used to define group priors. PFM methods included Independent Components Analysis and Dual Regression (ICA-DR), Probabilistic Functional Modes (ProFuMo), Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF), Multi-Session Hierarchical Bayesian Modeling (MS-HBM), and Template Matching (TM). Methods were independently performed at a 14-network dimensionality. After subtracting the group mean, Sørensen-Dice scores were calculated separately on vertices where the subject’s network was larger (positive dice score) or smaller (negative dice score) than the group. Ward’s hierarchical clustering on group template networks (non-demeaned) revealed 9 out of 14 networks with close correspondence in all PFM methods (dice 0.42-0.93), which were included in further analyses. All PFM methods showed high test-retest reliability and similarity between monozygotic (MZ) and dizygotic (DZ) twins (Fig. 1A). When comparing network boundaries between PFM methods, the highest similarity was observed between ICA-DR and ProFuMo and between TM and MS-HBM (Fig. 1B), and similar network features were qualitatively observed at the subject level (Fig. 1C). These results demonstrate that despite large differences in methodological approaches, these PFM methods capture similar network topographies and individual differences.

abstract:
Monocular deprivation (MD) is a classic paradigm to induce experience-dependent plasticity in rodents. In humans, MYT1L deficits cause neurodevelopmental diagnoses (NDDs), such as Intellectual Disability and autism. MYT1L syndrome is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the proneural transcription factor MYT1L. Patients with the loss-of-function mutation in MYT1L exhibit many types of developmental anomalies. Using critical period monocular deprivation as a model to drive experience-dependent plasticity, we first established WT mice’s responses to MD across three scales of investigation: gene expression and excitatory postsynaptic adaptations in the visual cortex and network-level resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) in the cortex. The highly stereotyped trajectory of the response to MD in the visual system makes it a good model to evaluate the roles of genetic mutations on experience-dependent plasticity.In gene expression, we found that MD downregulates visual cortex IEG expression in both WT and MYT1L-het mice. In physiological studies, we found that prolonged MD in WT mice caused a biphasic change in excitatory postsynaptic strength. Opposite to WT mice, mean visual cortex mEPSC amplitudes in MYT1L-het mice failed to undergo a reduction following MD2 (two days post MD) and trended toward a reduction at 6d MD. Beyond the visual cortex, we measured rsFC using wide-field fluorescence optical imaging (WFOI) and found that MYT1L mutation disrupts the network properties associated with experience-based plasticity that are seen in the WT MD mice when comparing delta calcium power and resting state functional connectivity. We found that, across all scales the response of MYT1L mice was substantially disrupted, indicating that the system cannot adapt.

abstract:
Opioid use disorder (OUD) is a chronic, relapsing condition that is marked by enduring neuroplastic changes. A hallmark of OUD is drug intake despite negative consequences; while most individuals will self-administer opioids and stop when a punishment is introduced (punishment-sensitive; PS), a subset will persist (punishment-resistant; PR). This along with the severe physical and affective symptoms induced by cessation of opioids renders abstinence difficult to achieve.
Therefore, elucidating these molecular changes is critical to identifying novel therapeutics to treat OUD. The ventral pallidum (VP) is a central node in the basal ganglia, and its activity is necessary for opioid seeking and relapse. Despite this, little is known about how opioids modulate plasticity in the VP, and how this may lead to persistent changes in opioid-seeking.
We developed a high throughput homecage oxycodone (OXY) self-administration paradigm that enabled us to test the punishment sensitivity of mice by pairing OXY with a probabilistic air puff. Like human populations, we found that most mice stopped OXY intake (PS), which a subset continued (PR). We found that punishment sensitivity is dissociable from opioid re-seeking after withdrawal, which suggests multiple forms of behavioural plasticity converge in the VP. To this end, we molecularly profiled the VP and its projections and identified several opioid-sensitive neuronal populations. Amongst these was an inhibitory Bnc2-expressing cluster that projects to the VTA, which distinguishes PR from PS mice. These results suggest that transcriptional remodelling of VP Bnc2+ neurons modulates VTA responses to reward, biasing mice towards more persistent seeking despite punishment. Consistent with multiple forms of opioid-induced behavioural plasticity, we also identified neuronal clusters implicated in withdrawal, which are distinct from the cluster involved in PR OXY consumption. Differential gene expression highlighted a vGlut2+ subpopulation as maximally affected by acute withdrawal. Through selective ablation, we determined that these neurons are essential to the development of withdrawal symptoms and OXY re-seeking after withdrawal. Given the previously described role of these cells in aversion, our results suggest that VP vGlut2 activity is increased during withdrawal, driving the aversive state that leads to maladaptive seeking and relapse.
Together, this work provides critical insight into the cellular heterogeneity of the VP and identifies several neuronal populations as important targets in treating maladaptive opioid seeking across multiple facets in OUD.

abstract: Ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs) are critical for excitatory neurotransmission in the central nervous system, particularly during neuronal development. Gain- and loss-of-function mutations in iGluRs genes have been shown to impair neuronal development and neuronal activity. In particular, reports have shown that the A657T pathogenic variant in the GRIK2 kainate receptor (KAR) gene causes neurodevelopmental deficits in mice and humans. Biophysical analysis of ion channel kinetics shows significantly impaired channel function, as evidenced by decreased current amplitude, reduced percent desensitization, and a slower rate of desensitization. Recently, parents of individuals harboring the A657T mutation reported that these individuals exhibit profound sensory deficits, characterized by decreased sensitivity to touch, pain, and itch. Whether the GRIK2-A657T mutation also affects the peripheral nervous system and impairs somatosensation remains unknown. Using a battery of sensory tests, we showed that mice harboring the pathogenic A657T mutation exhibit significant deficits in detecting noxious cold and heat and in nocifensive behaviors in response to inflammatory pain. In addition, Grik2A657T mice exhibit a profound decrease in touch sensitivity. In vivo calcium imaging DRG recordings from awake mice showed that DRG neurons from Grik2A657T mice had a significant increase in overall transient-stimulus-evoked calcium activity during noxious heat, cold, and innocuous mechanical stimulation compared to DRG neurons from WT mice. In addition, we found a significant decrease in sustained stimulus-evoked calcium activity in DRG neurons from Grik2A657T mice, in response to noxious cold stimulation, compared to DRG neurons from WT mice. This study provides the first in vivo evidence of dysregulated peripheral somatosensation and sensory neuron dysfunction due to mutant GluK2 receptors. Understanding how aberrant GluK2 signaling impairs somatosensation could help us develop new strategies to treat conditions that alter mechanosensation, thermosensation, and nociception.

abstract: Primary somatosensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) use highly specialized receptors to detect touch, temperature, pressure, vibration, and pain and transform these external stimuli into electrical signals. DRG neurons form synapses with second-order neurons in the spinal cord and encode the appropriate sensory modality to each type of tactile input by projecting to functionally and anatomically distinct laminae in the dorsal horn. A unique population of DRG neurons, called C-fiber low threshold mechanoreceptors (C-LTMRs), synapse exclusively onto interneurons in lamina II and transmit pleasurable light touch stimuli. However, it remains unknown how C-LTMRs determine synaptic partner choice during development, allowing them to encode light touch. C-LTMRs are the only population of DRG neurons that express cadherin 9 (Cdh9) and cadherin 10 (Cdh10). Cadherins are a family of synaptic adhesion and recognition molecules that identify neurons as target binding partners within developing circuits. Given that the loss of individual cadherins disrupts synaptic organization in other sensory circuits, we hypothesized that Cdh9/10 serve as critical determinants of synaptic connectivity at primary C-LTMR synapses in the spinal cord. To test this, we acquired mice with a global knockout of the group II cadherins Cdh6, Cdh9, and Cdh10 and assessed the density of C-LTMR synapses in the dorsal horn and sensitivity to light touch stimuli in these mice. We found that mice lacking Cdh6/9/10 had decreased expression of VGLUT3, a selective marker of C-LTMR axon terminals, in lamina II of the dorsal horn. These mice also displayed decreased sensitivity to C-LTMR selective stimuli, suggesting a deficit in light touch encoding in the absence of Cdh6/9/10. Future experiments will explore the anatomical, functional, and behavioral effects of deleting Cdh9/10 exclusively in C-LTMRs during sensory neuron development. This study provides significant insight into the role of cell type-specific cadherins in mediating somatosensory circuit assembly.

abstract: Human cortical neurogenesis is an intricate, tightly managed process centrally controlled by transcriptional regulatory networks. As major components of these networks, transcription factors (TFs) orchestrate pivotal cellular fate transitions during neurogenesis, including the differentiation of neural progenitor cells (NPCs) into neurons. Our prior work derived an epigenetic atlas by which to identify novel TFs that bind cis-regulatory elements (CREs) during cortical interneuron development. Focusing on the transition of human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived medial ganglionic eminence-like (MGE) progenitors into cortical interneurons, we identified Regulatory Factor X (RFX) 2, 3, and 4 as key regulators of neurogenesis — results of particular interest considering the recent designation of RFX 3, 4, and 7 as autism spectrum disorder risk genes. Motivated by its temporally restricted expression in NPCs, our latest work sought to characterize the regulatory functions of RFX4. We found that RFX4 restrains the onset of neuronal gene expression during both GABAergic and glutamatergic neurogenesis and functions downstream of NOTCH signaling to repress pro-neuronal and synaptic gene expression. We also found that RFX3 requires RFX4 for genome-wide binding, while others have shown that RFX TFs form homo- and heterodimers with themselves and other RFX family members. Taken together, these data suggest coordination between the RFX TFs to regulate developmental processes during cortical neurogenesis. However, the exact mechanisms by which RFX TFs control cortical development, including how they interact with both each other and other TFs, remain largely unknown. Here, we have derived CRISPRi models to enable the knockdown of RFX 1, 2, 5, and 7 in hPSCs. Complementing their differentiation into GABAergic and glutamatergic NPCs with transcriptomic, epigenetic, and cellular phenotyping analyses, we have profiled the consequences of RFX knockdown during progenitor specification and begun to characterize the functional relationships between RFX4 and the other RFX TFs. Ultimately, this work will elucidate requirements for the RFX TFs during cortical development and inform our understanding of neurodevelopmental disorders caused by mutations in the RFX genes.

abstract: The nuclear factor one (NFI) family of transcription factors consists of NFIA, NFIB, NFIC, and NFIX. In humans and mice, NFIA, NFIB, and NFIX are expressed at high levels in the cerebral cortex during development as well as adulthood. Haploinsufficiency of NFIA, NFIB, and NFIX results in human neurodevelopmental syndromes that share characteristic features with another neurodevelopmental syndrome caused by transcription factor 4 (TCF4) haploinsufficiency. Shared phenotypes between NFI and TCF4 haploinsufficiency syndromes include intellectual disability, developmental delay, and dysgenesis of the corpus callosum. These overlapping phenotypes indicate that NFIA, NFIB, NFIX, and TCF4 haploinsufficiency syndromes may have similar underlying etiologies. Additionally, recent transcriptomic, epigenomic, and proteomic studies suggest that NFIB and TCF4 may converge by binding to the same cis-regulatory elements and regulate a common set of target genes as a result. Given the shared phenotypes of NFI and TCF4 haploinsufficiency syndromes and the evidence supporting molecular convergence, we investigated whether NFIB and TCF4 converge by regulating similar target genes during neocortical development. We compared bulk RNA-seq data of embryonic day 13.5 (E13.5) Nfib knockout (KO) and E14.5 Tcf4 KO mouse cortical tissue and found a large overlapping set of downregulated genes involved in neuronal differentiation. We next performed Cleavage Under Targets & Release Using Nuclease (CUT&RUN) on E14.5 neocortical tissue to identify genome-wide binding of NFIB and TCF4. This revealed over 6000 shared binding sites across the genome. We further hypothesized that NFIB and TCF4 may physically interact with each other to bind to these regulatory elements. Therefore, we are currently performing GST-pulldown experiments to test this hypothesis. These ongoing experiments could reveal how these transcription factors function to regulate similar target genes and identify potential mechanisms underlying NFI and TCF4 haploinsufficiency syndromes.

abstract: Background: Primary and secondary tauopathies are characterized by progressive impairments in neuronal activity, network synchrony, and excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) imbalance. Despite extensive investigation of tau-mediated neuronal dysfunction, considerably less is known about how these changes impact the neurovascular unit and coupling. Our previous studies demonstrate that tau pathology disrupts sleep, reduces EEG beta power, alters glutamate and GABA production, and promotes cortical hyperexcitability, suggesting widespread network dysfunction. Importantly, inhibitory signaling remains a plausible therapeutic target. Because coordinated neuronal activity is a primary regulator of cerebral blood flow, we hypothesized that tau-dependent E/I imbalance contributed to neurovascular uncoupling. Methods: EEG/EMG recordings were performed on 9 month P301S and wildtype (WT) mice to assess sleep quantity, relative frequency, and oscillatory activity. Stable isotope-resolved metabolomics quantifies glucose-derived and total metabolite abundance. Wide-field optical imaging (WFOI) measured glutamatergic calcium dynamics and hemodynamics during rest and stimulation. Immunohistochemistry characterized inhibitory neuronal populations and vascular morphology. Results: Tau pathology reduces time spent in NREM and REM sleep while reducing EEG beta power, coherence, and altering oscillatory activity. Metabolomics revealed an overall reduction in metabolite abundance; however, P301S mice exhibited an increase in 13C labeled glutamate at the expense of GABA production. WFOI revealed increased glutamatergic calcium dynamics during stimulation in P301S mice. Despite heightened neuronal activity, P301S mice exhibited abnormal hemodynamic responses. Lectin labeling of brain vasculature revealed increased branching, length, and thickness of vessels. Additionally, preliminary data suggests P301S mice exhibit reductions in parvalbumin labeled neurons and GAD65/67 labeling. Conclusions: Tau pathology is associated with progressive network dysfunction characterized by E/I imbalance, metabolic reprogramming, impaired synchrony, and neurovascular uncoupling. Our findings support a model in which tau pathology disrupts inhibitory regulation of cerebral hemodynamics. Ongoing studies using whole-brain light sheet microscopy and single-nucleus RNA sequencing will define how tau pathology alters neuronal populations, vascular architecture, and cell-type specific transcriptional programs. Identifying mechanisms linking neuronal and vascular dysfunction may reveal novel therapeutic targets for tauopathies.

abstract: Myelin, a lipid-rich sheath that insulates axons, is thought to be neuroprotective, though the mechanisms underlying this protection remain unclear. To directly address this, we developed a mouse model where myelin is spatially restricted to the posterior optic nerve (ON), leaving the anterior region completely unmyelinated. After ON transection, we observed accelerated Wallerian degeneration (WD) in unmyelinated regions of the nerves compared to myelinated regions both 3- and 6-days post injury. This accelerated WD was not mediated by microglia since their ablation did not affect degeneration. While proteomics of unmyelinated ON regions showed no obvious differences in degeneration-related targets compared to myelinated regions, metabolomics revealed distinct changes linked to SARM1-mediated degeneration. Importantly, in mice with partially myelinated ONs but also lacking SARM1, degeneration was no longer accelerated, suggesting that myelin protects axons from degeneration by suppressing SARM1 activity. These findings reveal a new link between myelin and SARM1-mediated degeneration and provide insight into local axonal protection mechanisms that may guide future therapies for neurodegenerative diseases.

abstract: Postoperative pain and opioid use remain major challenges following elective spine surgery, highlighting the need for non-pharmacological interventions that target the neural mechanisms of pain. Peak alpha frequency (PAF), the dominant frequency of resting-state electroencephalographic (EEG) alpha oscillations (8-13 Hz), has emerged as a reliable, trait-like biomarker of individual pain sensitivity; slower PAF is associated with heightened pain sensitivity, whereas faster PAF is linked to greater pain tolerance. Despite robust observational evidence connecting PAF to pain outcomes in both experimental and clinical populations, no study has investigated whether PAF can be deliberately modified as a therapeutic target or whether such modification can improve postoperative outcomes. To address this gap, we conducted a randomized study of 39 adult patients (mean age 66.9 years, male & female) undergoing elective spine surgery to test whether preoperative 8 Hz auditory stimulation could shift PAF and reduce postoperative pain and opioid consumption. Patients were randomized to receive daily preoperative 8 Hz auditory stimulation (treatment, n=22) or sham stimulation (n=7). Eyes-closed resting-state EEG was recorded at three time points: enrollment, day of surgery, and day of discharge. PAF was derived using a center-of-gravity approach applied to detrended alpha-band power spectra. Treatment patients were stratified by baseline PAF into Slow (<10.1 Hz) and Fast (≥10.1 Hz) groups. Auditory stimulation produced bidirectional modulation of PAF: the Slow group increased (p=0.014) and the Fast group decreased (p=0.003), converging symmetrically toward ~10 Hz, whereas sham patients showed no significant change (p=0.375). In the Slow group, preoperative listening reduced VAS neck/back pain prior to surgery (p=0.004), and by postoperative day 3, pain levels had fallen below baseline values (p=0.031). The magnitude of individual PAF increase was strongly associated with reduced postoperative opioid consumption (r=−0.866, p=0.001), and a dose-response relationship was observed between preoperative listening duration and PAF shift magnitude (r=0.688, p=0.019). These findings provide the first evidence that PAF is not merely a static biomarker of pain susceptibility but a modifiable therapeutic target, and that a simple, home-based auditory intervention administered preoperatively can induce neurophysiological changes that translate into meaningful clinical benefits for spine surgery patients.

abstract: The ventromedial medulla (VMM) is a brainstem region containing essential subnuclei implicated in the descending modulation of pain and pelvic musculature through spinal circuits. Neuroanatomical studies have shown that the ventromedial medulla is multi-synaptically connected to urinary bladder afferents, and canonical ventromedial medullary “ON” and “OFF” cells have been identified in response to bladder distention. Still, these studies have not been able to provide refined VMM molecular cell types, connectivity and activity defined atlas that may be leveraged to build mechanistic insights into bladder overactivity and pain. To identify ventromedial medulla neuronal types and projections that are involved in bladder pain and dysfunction, we employed a high-resolution multimodal map of the mouse VMM that combines spatial organization, molecular profiling, and projection patterns of medulla neurons. We combined this refined atlas of the VMM with transcriptomic sequencing of immediate early genes to identify activated or silenced cell types in the VMM in response to cystitis. Using retrograde virus injections, we identify neurons within these clusters that specifically project to the lumbosacral spinal cord, a crucial site for the integration of bladder somatosensation. By implementing computational ethology on 3D kinematic representations of freely moving mice, we show that modulation of these neurons recapitulates spontaneous pain behaviors seen uniquely in cystitis. This refined molecular and neuroanatomical understanding of the ventromedial medulla is an essential foundation for the development of specific, targeted pharmacology in the treatment of cystitis.

abstract: The cone-rod homeobox (CRX) is a transcription factor regulating the development and survival of rod and cone photoreceptors. Human CRXE80A mutation in the homeodomain is linked to autosomal dominant early-onset cone-rod dystrophy (CoRD). Our previous studies reported that early-onset cone loss in CrxE80A/+ knock-in mouse model recapitulated CoRD-like manifestations. CrxE80A mutation downregulated the expression of rod genes while severely disrupted the transcription regulation of cone genes. This study aimed to track cell fate of the cone lineage in CrxE80A/+ mice and to develop gene therapy. We utilized Thrbb2Cre+/-; Ai6 reporter line to label fated cones in green, and immunohistochemistry (IHC) on established cone identity markers, RXRG, ARR3 and cone opsins, at postnatal day 0 (P0), P10, P14, P21 and P30. We found that cones are co-labeled by the Ai6 reporter and IHC of cone markers in WT retinae at all tested ages. In contrast, CrxE80A/+ cones show co-labelling at P0, but progressively lose cone markers during postnatal differentiation, becoming only detectable by the Ai6 reporter by P30. These data suggest that CrxE80A/+ cones remain viable through young adulthood despite losing cone identity during development. We further tested if CrxE80A/+ mutation caused a similar loss of cone identity in cone-enriched Nrl-/-;pNrl-GFP retinae in which Nrl knockout converted rods into cone-like cells. During photoreceptor differentiation, all cells in outer nuclear layers of Nrl-/-;pNrl-GFP retinae were co-labeled by GFP and IHC of cone markers; however, CrxE80A/+ mutation greatly decreased the population of co-label cells. CRX augmentation, the overexpression of functional CRX, may serve as a viable treatment strategy for CRXE80A mutation. We evaluated the therapeutic potential of AAV2.7m8-pCrx-CRX via subretinal injection of 1011vg/mL into the CrxE80A/+;Thrbb2Cre+/-;Ai6 retinae at two treatment windows: P14 to P28, a period of progressive loss in cone identity during photoreceptor differentiation; P30 to P44, a period of absent cone identity. This therapeutic intervention resulted in co-labeled cones in treated CrxE80A/+;Thrbb2Cre+/-;Ai6 retinae at both treatment windows. These preclinical data suggest that AAV-mediated CRX augmentation not only preserves cone identity during development but also recovers lost identity in underdeveloped cones in young adulthood. Altogether, this study highlights the importance of maintaining cell identity as a key therapeutic goal and unveils the potential plasticity of treatment windows for gene therapy.

abstract: The fusiform gyrus (FG) encodes visual features to represent face identities, yet how these representations are transmitted to downstream regions to support distinct cognitive demands remains poorly understood. Here, we combined intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) and single-neuron recordings in neurosurgical patients, as well as fMRI in healthy participants during face viewing, to characterize how the FG is functionally embedded within the distributed face-processing network. Consistent with recent intracranial studies, we identified FG channels that linearly encoded feature axes, exhibiting axis-based feature coding. These axis-coding channels showed markedly stronger theta-band (3-8 Hz) phase synchronization than non-axis-coding FG channels with a distributed set of higher-order face-processing regions, including the amygdala, superior temporal sulcus (STS), medial temporal gyrus (MTG), medial temporal cortex (MTC), ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC), and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), beginning shortly after stimulus onset. At the cellular level, neurons in the amygdala and hippocampus were preferentially phase-locked to FG axis-coding channels, indicating that local FG visual codes are read out by medial temporal lobe (MTL) neurons through low-frequency coherence. Critically, FG connectivity reorganized as a function of the information being processed: familiarity-coding channels in the amygdala and OFC showed stronger synchronization with FG, and at the single-neuron level, hippocampal but not amygdala neurons exhibited familiarity-enhanced phase locking with the FG, OFC, and VLPFC. Social trait-coding channels in the amygdala, rostral middle frontal cortex (RFC), and OFC showed stronger FG synchronization, while the thalamus and dorsal pathway, including the inferior parietal lobule (IPL) and superior parietal lobule (SPL), exhibited stronger desynchronization. Phase slope index analyses revealed that feedforward signaling from FG to downstream regions dominated these interactions across both identity and familiarity networks. Independent fMRI functional connectivity analyses converged on this network architecture. Together, these findings identify the FG as a flexible routing hub that dynamically coordinates with distinct downstream targets depending on whether visual identity, familiarity, or social trait is being computed. Our results provide a multimodal, multiscale framework that links localized visual feature representations to distributed circuits, supporting flexible perception, memory, and social cognition.

abstract: Localized visual features are encoded within the ventral temporal cortex (VTC) to represent object identities, yet how these representations are dynamically routed to downstream regions to flexibly support distinct cognitive demands remains a fundamental question. Integrating human intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) and single-neuron recordings in neurosurgical patients with functional MRI in healthy participants, we map the multiscale network architecture embedding the VTC during object viewing. We demonstrate that VTC channels exhibiting axis-based feature coding act as communication hubs; shortly after stimulus onset, these channels initiate robust theta-band (4-8 Hz) phase synchronization with a distributed set of higher-order object-processing regions, explicitly involving the amygdala, insula, superior temporal sulcus (STS), middle temporal gyrus (MTG), medial temporal cortex (MTC), ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC), orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), and rostral middle frontal cortex (RFC). At the cellular level, individual neurons in the amygdala and hippocampus preferentially phase-lock to these axis-coding VTC channels, providing direct evidence that local visual codes are read out via low-frequency coherence. Specifically, this routing architecture flexibly reorganizes as a function of cognitive demand: when processing behavioral memorability, memorability-coding channels within the amygdala, OFC, and STS selectively amplify their synchronization with the VTC. At the single-neuron level, this cognitive modulation manifests as memorability-enhanced phase locking within distinct sub-circuits—specifically between amygdala neurons and the VTC, OFC, and between hippocampal neurons and the VTC, insula. To validate these patterns, we examined convergent functional connectivity in an independent NSD fMRI dataset, confirming that axis-coding FG voxels show elevated connectivity with frontal areas. This supports the view of the VTC as a flexible routing engine. Depending on whether the task demands processing visual identity or memorability, the VTC selectively engages different downstream targets, demonstrating how localized visual representations plug into large-scale circuits to guide flexible thought.

abstract: Inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA) produce motivational deficits — reduced effort, withdrawal from rewarding pursuits — that are clinically distinct from pain yet poorly understood mechanistically. Here, using the K/BxN serum transfer arthritis model and multiple motivation-related behavior tasks, we show that experimental inflammatory arthritis in mice induces a selective deficit in foraging and effortful reward-seeking. Arthritis-derived cytokines act on vagal afferents of the nodose ganglion: conditional deletion of their receptors in vagal sensory neurons improves motivation without altering joint inflammation. Vagal input recruits the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) and its downstream projections, and silencing the projection partially restores motivation in progressive-ratio performance. In healthy mice, optogenetic activation of the NTS recruits pathways that suppress dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens. These findings define a body-to-brain interoceptive circuit that converts peripheral inflammation into amotivation by gating dopaminergic drive, identifying a tractable target for inflammation-associated behavioral symptoms.

abstract:
Background: Negative interpretation bias -- the tendency to perceive ambiguous stimuli as threatening -- is a core cognitive distortion underlying post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The amygdala, a key structure in fear processing, is implicated in PTSD-related hypervigilance and heightened fear perception, yet direct causal evidence linking amygdala function to negative interpretation bias remains limited.
Methods: We present a unique prospective case of a male index patient with refractory epilepsy and comorbid chronic PTSD, who underwent stereoelectroencephalography-guided radiofrequency ablation (SEEG-guided RFA) targeting the right amygdala. The index patient and 16 control subjects also performed a facial emotion discrimination task.
Results: Before ablation, the patient exhibited heightened negative interpretation bias, judging ambiguous faces as more fearful compared to control groups of epilepsy patients without PTSD. Intracranial SEEG recordings revealed that this cognitive bias was associated with increased late-phase event-related potential (L-ERP) differentiation between fearful and happy faces in the right amygdala. Immediately following focal right amygdala ablation, negative interpretation bias and PTSD symptom severity were significantly reduced, while seizure frequency remained unchanged. Notably, reductions in L-ERP amplitude after ablation closely tracked decreases in fear perception, highlighting L-ERP as a potential biomarker of negative interpretation bias and therapeutic response.
Conclusions: Our findings provide causal evidence from an n-of-1 study that the right amygdala supports maladaptive negative interpretation bias in a patient with PTSD and that right amygdala ablation can contribute to the relief of PTSD symptomatology.

abstract: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) represents contexts using distinct patterns of activity. These context representations are used by the lateral PFC to maintain relevant information in working memory (WM) and by the medial PFC to retrieve context-congruent episodic memories (EM) via interactions with the hippocampus. While work continues to elucidate PFC function and circuitry, the computational mechanisms by which context modulates memory is less understood. To address this, we designed several context modulation models and compared them against naturalistic fMRI data (Song et al., 2025). Recurrent neural networks (RNN) were trained to receive audiovisual inputs from movie scenes at each time step and predict semantics of the next scene, including characters present and time and location. Models were trained on all but one episode of This Is Us Season 1 and tested on the held-out episode. Episodes consisted of four interleaved character narratives. The narrative each scene belonged to served as a context signal provided during training. At test, the model inferred context via Bayesian inference. The model in which context modulated WM (i.e., the RNN recurrence) in a low-rank manner (Mastroguiseppe & Ostojic, 2018) achieved the highest representational similarity to cortical activity of fMRI participants who watched the same episode, outperforming RNN variants in which context modulated either inputs or outputs, and a model without low-rank constraints. This suggests that WM may be gated by contexts through low-rank modulation of connectivity in the lateral PFC. Turning to EM, we augmented this WM-modulated RNN with an EM buffer that encodes and retrieves memories via self-attention. In addition to encoding scene contents, the inferred context was encoded into the EM at every time step, and pattern similarity between past and current contexts was computed. This context similarity was multiplied by the self-attention outcome (i.e., content similarity), biasing retrieval of context-congruent memories. Of all EM variants tested, this model exhibited the most human-like memory retrieval. This benefit was most pronounced early in learning and observed only when both WM and EM were modulated. This architecture simulates the mPFC-hippocampus interaction, where the hippocampus encodes both content and context information and the mPFC uses context representations to selectively retrieve congruent memories. Together, our results suggest that context modulates WM by engaging different low-rank connectivity and EM by preferentially retrieving context-congruent memories—shedding light on the functional roles of the lateral and medial PFC, respectively.

abstract: Human and animal behavior unfolds across short and long timescales. A driver returning from work may react to a changing traffic light while simultaneously being guided by slower internal conditions—such as engagement with external stimuli and responsiveness to them, commonly referred to as arousal. Arousal can shift flexibly, even abruptly, and is thought to rely on widespread, coordinated neural processes. Yet which large-scale spiking regimes instantiate arousal-related internal states, and how they are coordinated across the brain, remain unclear. Functional connectivity (FC) measured by fMRI and local field potentials is known to fluctuate with arousal and reflect multi-region coordination, but how neuron-level FC changes across long-range connections and how such changes are coordinated across brain areas remains unclear. The mediodorsal (MD) thalamus is a compelling candidate for this coordinating role: it projects broadly to prefrontal areas important for regulating internal states, including the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and ventral lateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC). While MD neurons are sensitive to arousal states, how MD activity regulates prefrontal networks remains unclear. To study the neuronal basis of arousal, we recorded population activity from MD and its downstream prefrontal areas, ACC and VLPFC, and examined FC across them. We found distinct ACC-VLPFC FC patterns across arousal states: neurons fired more synchronously in rest-like states, resulting in increased FC. Surprisingly, neuron-by-neuron FC patterns were uncorrelated across arousal states, suggesting a state-dependent functional structure. Crucially, MD inactivation causally exerted state-dependent remapping in prefrontal FC and unexpectedly produced new functional connections. Post-inactivation networks were similar to each other but different from pre-inactivation states. We next investigated how MD inactivation may cause these changes through detailed analyses of MD neurons and computational modelling. We found that MD neurons shift from uncorrelated firing to synchronized population bursty patterns, producing large-scale, low-dimensional thalamic states during rest-like state. A spiking network further uncovered how thalamic synchrony induces different prefrontal connectivity across states. Modelling shows that a specific thalamocortical projection structure is required to recapitulate our results. In vivo retrograde tracing results supported this structure. Overall, our results reveal a thalamus-driven mechanism for coordinating distributed prefrontal networks and structuring the architecture of internal states.

abstract: Humans and other primates can perform and rapidly switch between many tasks. Prefrontal cortex (PFC) has been implicated in task representation, with baseline firing rates differing across tasks. We used a neural geometry approach to ask whether PFC baseline activity (1) is organized or is idiosyncratic across neuronal populations; (2) encodes a single task-related variable or multiple; and (3) anticipates task performance or follows from it. We trained two rhesus monkeys to perform six cognitive tasks in explicitly cued, 16-trial blocks, and recorded hundreds of neurons per session with a Neuropixels probe in the frontal eye field, dorsolateral PFC, or premotor cortex. Mean firing rates were analyzed during an initial 1-s fixation period before any task-relevant stimulus or planned response, isolating activity that could only reflect task context. In each area, population baseline activity for each task occupied a distinct location in a neural subspace (i.e., “task space”) and the upcoming task could be decoded from a single held-out trial, while decoding accuracy was degraded on error trials, linking the population state to behavior. The task space was multidimensional, with each dimension carrying independent information; no single global factor such as reward rate or difficulty could account for the geometry. Remarkably, consistent task geometry was observed across independently sampled neuronal populations, providing evidence of a shared organizing principle rather than an idiosyncratic representation. This shared geometry was strongly conserved within an area but only partly across areas, suggesting each frontal region may configure a distinct preparatory state. Still, such geometry could reflect the task just completed rather than anticipate the one to come. Examining trial-by-trial dynamics revealed that the population state switched abruptly on the very first trial of a new block, before the task had been performed, and persisted when the explicit color cue was removed mid-block, indicating that the population state encodes the upcoming task rather than the color cue or an echo of prior performance. Together, these findings support a model in which frontal cortex holds a rich, structured representation of task context that is partially area-specific, analogous to motor preparatory activity, but for cognitive tasks.

abstract:
Genetically defined deep-brain populations mediate motivation, adaptive behavior, and disease-related circuit remodeling, yet how these populations reorganize across distributed brain regions remains poorly understood. Progress has been limited by the challenge of repeatedly monitoring deep-brain populations with genetic specificity while preserving intact brain physiology. With current technologies, long‑term, non‑invasive imaging of genetically defined deep‑brain circuits remains a key unmet goal. Non-invasive imaging modalities such as functional MRI provide brain-wide access but lack cellular specificity and have limited temporal resolution, whereas genetically encoded fluorescent reporters provide cell-type specificity but are constrained by tissue scattering and limited optical access to deep structures. Near-infrared (NIR) fluorescent proteins offer improved tissue penetration compared with visible-wavelength reporters, but currently available NIR fluorescent proteins remain limited by insufficient brightness and in vivo sensitivity for deep-brain imaging.
To address this challenge, we developed NIR20e, a next-generation NIR fluorescent protein engineered through genome mining of bacteriophytochrome sequences combined with machine-learning-guided protein design. Biophysical characterization demonstrated substantially improved brightness and photostability relative to the current state-of-the-art NIR fluorescent protein. In mice, we introduced viral NIR20e expression and used a custom wide-field NIR imaging system to demonstrate non-invasive, through-scalp fluorescence detection from deep-brain structures. Compared with GFP, NIR20e enabled robust transcranial visualization of striatal and nucleus accumbens signals through intact scalp and skull. Furthermore, NIR20e expression in midbrain dopaminergic neurons demonstrated transcranial detection of sparse, genetically defined deep-brain populations.
Longitudinal NIR imaging also enabled visualization of neurodegeneration dynamics in a kainic-acid model of hippocampal injury. Repeated transcranial imaging captured progressive neuronal signal loss and delayed bilateral changes consistent with circuit-level reorganization, demonstrating the utility of NIR20e for longitudinal tracking of distributed circuit remodeling within the same animal.
Together, these findings establish NIR20e as a versatile genetically encoded reporter for non-invasive, longitudinal imaging of genetically defined deep-brain circuits and distributed neural populations.

abstract:
There is a pressing need for the development of non-genetic techniques that allow reversible control of neural responses. Here, we develop and demonstrate a novel approach based on mesoporous silica-coated polydopamine nanoparticles (mSiO2@PDA NPs) that can function both as nanoheaters, enabling precise focal heating via the photothermal effect, and as nanocarriers, enabling controlled local release of a desired chemical payload to modulate neural activity in a target circuit. We demonstrate this targeted chemo-photothermal neuromodulation approach in the locust (Schistocerca americana).
We delivered mSiO2@PDA NPs onto a specific olfactory neural circuit (antennal lobe or AL; analogous to vertebrate olfactory bulb). Combining odor delivery with optical stimulation of octopamine-loaded mSiO2@PDA NPs enabled tunable gain control of neural signals, amplifying both odor-evoked neural responses and final behavioral outcomes. We show that while odor-evoked responses are altered, the identity of the odor (combination of neurons activated) and the type of behavioral response elicited are preserved. We demonstrate modulation of two types of odor-evoked behavioral responses: an appetitive response (opening maxillary palps near the mouth) and a navigational response (walking). Reversible modulation of both the probability of the behavioral response as well as the intensity of behavioral response (i.e., walking speed) was observed.
Interestingly, even direct chemo-photothermal modulation of mSiO2@PDA NPs without odor delivery elicited neural activity in the targeted antennal lobe circuit. These ‘phantom’ odorants produced behavioral effects similar to those evoked by the natural olfactory stimuli and could be used to evoke both appetitive and walking behavior in locusts. In sum, our results establish chemo-photothermal neuromodulation as a minimally invasive, non-genetic framework for neural and behavioral control.

abstract: The ability to manipulate information in mind is a defining feature of human cognition, but the neuronal mechanisms that enable this capacity remain unclear. We leveraged the high spatiotemporal fidelity of human intracranial recordings to examine how the brain transforms mentally held object sequences. In an auditory working memory task (N = 30), mental manipulation evoked an increase in medial-temporal (MTL) lower-frequency dynamics and enhanced directed theta-alpha synchrony (6-10 Hz), especially between auditory, prefrontal, and hippocampal areas. The strength of this coupling predicted imagery vividness and task performance. In parallel, the tonic activity of individually-recorded MTL neurons discriminated between conditions, suggesting a different excitability state during mental manipulation compared to simple recall. In a separate visual working memory experiment (N = 12), cued mental manipulation enhanced delay-period persistent firing of image-selective MTL neurons. Crucially, selective neurons tended to fire in forward sequences during simple recall and backward sequences during temporal inversion with respect to the position of their preferred image during encoding. These findings suggest that mental manipulation relies on distributed lower-frequency control dynamics and reconfiguration of neural sequences via intentional replay.

abstract:
Approach-avoidance conflict requires balancing reward seeking against potential threat and is a core feature of adaptive behavior and anxiety-related disorders. Although autonomic arousal is known to influence decision-making during threat, the neural circuits linking threat processing to autonomic state changes in humans remain poorly understood. Here, we combined intracranial electrophysiological recordings, pupillometry, and causal lesion data to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying autonomic arousal during approach-avoidance conflict.
Twenty-five neurosurgical patients performed a dynamic approach-avoidance task in which participants collected rewards while avoiding pursuit and attack by a virtual predator. Simultaneous eye tracking was used to quantify pupil diameter as an index of autonomic arousal. High-frequency activity (70-170 Hz) was extracted from intracranial recordings across cortical and subcortical regions. To assess causal contributions, a subset of participants completed the task both before and after radiofrequency ablation, including five patients with unilateral amygdala ablation and one patient with right anterior insula ablation.
Threat pursuit and attack elicited robust increases in pupil diameter compared with foraging periods. Across participants, high-frequency activity in the anterior insula and ventral thalamic regions significantly predicted trial-by-trial pupil dilation during threat encounters. Critically, the participant who underwent right anterior insula ablation exhibited a marked reduction in threat-evoked pupil dilation following ablation, providing causal evidence that the anterior insula contributes to autonomic arousal during approach-avoidance conflict. In contrast, unilateral amygdala ablation did not produce consistent changes in pupil responses or task behavior.
These findings identify the anterior insula as a key node linking threat processing to autonomic state changes in humans and suggest that pupil-linked arousal during defensive behavior is more closely associated with insular and thalamic circuits than with amygdala activity. By integrating intracranial recordings with causal perturbation, this study provides new insight into the neural mechanisms that transform threat into autonomic and behavioral responses during approach-avoidance conflict.

abstract: First impressions arise within fractions of a second from viewing a face, requiring a rapid transformation from visual representations of facial features to abstract social evaluations. How this sensory-to-social transformation unfolds across the human brain, and how it is altered in conditions of atypical social cognition, remains poorly understood. Using intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings from 31 neurotypical individuals, we characterized the spatiotemporal dynamics of this transformation during face viewing. Time-resolved partial representational similarity analysis revealed a dynamic propagation cascade in which visual feature representations emerged rapidly and broadly across the face-processing network, including higher-order social-evaluative regions. Over time, this initially distributed representation differentiated into a hierarchical organization, with visual feature encoding remaining strongest in posterior regions while social trait representations increasingly dominated higher-order social-evaluative. Directional connectivity analyses further indicated that information flow along this cascade was predominantly feedforward from the fusiform gyrus (FG). In two individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), iEEG recordings revealed a reorganized cascade characterized by reduced posterior face processing, enhanced encoding of visual facial features in frontal regions, and strengthened feedforward propagation. An independent fMRI cohort (25 ASD, 25 neurotypical participants) confirmed this spatial reorganization at the group level, showing reduced posterior and increased frontal responses, as well as enhanced FG-frontal connectivity during face processing in ASD. Together, these findings identify sensory-to-social propagation as a fundamental organizing principle of face-based social inference and suggest that this process is redistributed in ASD, with diminished engagement of specialized sensory regions accompanied by compensatory frontal recruitment. More broadly, the results provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how facial appearance is transformed into social meaning and how this transformation is altered in atypical social cognition.

abstract: Semaglutide (SEMA), a GLP-1R agonist prescribed for obesity and diabetes, reliably reduces food intake. While GLP-1R agonism regulates food intake, appetite, and glycemic control, it is increasingly recognized as regulating consumption behaviors across disorders, including alcohol and substance use disorder. This suggests SEMA may reduce consumption by broadly dampening motivation. However, how SEMA alters motivational and decision-making processes remains poorly understood. We addressed this in C57BL/6J mice using home cage operant assays: fixed-ratio (FR) responding, a closed-economy resetting progressive ratio (PR) task, probabilistic reversal learning, and passive infrared locomotor monitoring. Acute SEMA (0.025 mg/kg, IP) rapidly reduced FR responding for sucrose and decreased breakpoint, meal size, and total pellet consumption on the PR task without altering locomotor activity, arguing against generalized malaise. SEMA did not impair performance on a reversal learning task. Using a closed-economy task with a resetting progressive ratio schedule, we observed that SEMA decreased both food intake and willingness to exert effort for food. These effects occurred without changes in physical activity, indicating that reduced performance was likely not due to general malaise, although we did not rule out a role for gastrointestinal malaise in driving reductions in food intake. Computational reinforcement learning modeling revealed SEMA significantly shifted positive learning rates, negative learning rates, and choice-history weighting, yet reversal accuracy was preserved. SEMA-treated mice showed decreased Win-Stay and increased Lose-Shift behavior, indicating contingency learning was maintained while sensitivity to recent reward history was attenuated. To probe circuit mechanisms, we chemogenetically inhibited prelimbic cortex to nucleus accumbens (PL-NAc) projection neurons using cre-dependent hM4Di DREADDs. PL-NAc inhibition alone increased breakpoint without affecting reversal learning, establishing this projection as a selective brake on effortful food pursuit. Critically, PL-NAc inhibition rescued SEMA-induced reductions in food seeking by restoring meal size. The computational signature of SEMA was not replicated by PL-NAc inhibition alone, suggesting learning-rate effects arise via parallel mechanisms. These findings demonstrate that acute GLP-1R activation selectively constrains motivational drive without impairing adaptive decision-making, and identify PL-NAc circuitry as a necessary substrate for SEMA-induced reductions in effortful food seeking.

abstract: Chronic spinal cord injury (SCI) causes spinal networks below the level of injury to reorganize, often leading to SCI-related neuropathic pain (SCI-NP). Some clinical features of SCI-NP have a relatively intuitive neural underpinning, such as hyperalgesia and an increased responsiveness of spinal wide dynamic range and nociceptive-specific neurons to nociceptive sensory feedback. More enigmatic features of SCI-NP, such as allodynia and spontaneous pain, are less directly linked to changes in spinal neuron excitability. These features of SCI-NP may instead be represented by changes in the structure of neural population-level patterns of sensory transmission, which requires a different analytical framework and tools. Neural manifold analysis has emerged as a powerful approach to characterizing the population-level dynamics underlying complex sensorimotor and cognitive processes in brain networks. Although manifold analysis also holds considerable promise for characterizing spinal networks, this application is largely unexplored - particularly for sensory transmission. This study utilized a neural manifold framework to characterize spinal population-level sensory encoding, how it is altered by chronic SCI, and to determine whether and how clinical features of SCI-NP manifest at the manifold level. All studies were conducted in vivo in adult male Sprague Dawley rats, and all procedures were approved by the IACUC of Washington University in St. Louis. Microelectrode arrays were implanted into the lumbar enlargement of neurologically intact rats, those with chronic SCI-NP, and those with chronic SCI that lacked SCI-NP. Broadband intraspinal neural activity was recorded both during periods of innocuous and noxious cutaneous stimulation of the periphery and during quiescence. Single-unit activity was discriminated offline, and neurons were functionally classified according to their stimulus response. We then used PCA to transform the high-dimensional population activity into low-dimensional neural manifolds. In neurologically intact rats, population-level representations of nociceptive and non-nociceptive activity could be distinguished by spatiotemporal features of their respective manifolds. In rats with SCI, however, including those with SCI-NP, these distinctions became less apparent, suggesting a conflation of nociceptive and non-nociceptive encoding. These findings establish a framework for examining spinal sensory processing at the population level and provide insights into the mechanisms underlying SCI-NP.

abstract: Local field potentials (LFPs) provide a population-level measure of neuronal network activity and are widely used to characterize communication within and between supraspinal networks. In contrast, little is known about the physiological properties of intraspinal LFPs, largely due to the difficulty of obtaining stable recordings from spinal circuits during natural behavior. The purpose of this study is to delineate normative features of intraspinal LFPs in awake, behaving mice - an essential pre-requisite for understanding how spinal encoding is altered following injury.All procedures were approved by the WUSTL IACUC. Adult male C57BL/6 mice had ultraflexible microelectrode arrays implanted into their lumbar enlargement. The arrays spanned the dorsoventral extent of the spinal gray matter, enabling simultaneous recordings from sensory- to motor-dominant spinal regions. Extracellular recordings were acquired during sensory behavioral testing (Von Frey, Dry Ice, and Hargreaves test) and spontaneous behavior in awake, freely moving animals. Broadband neural activity was processed to extract local field potentials for spectral analyses.As an initial exploratory study, we sought to characterize the spectral features of intraspinal LFPs during natural behavior and compare them with recordings obtained under anesthesia. To quantify sensory-related modulation of intraspinal LFPs, we measured the area under the power spectral density curve across spinal regions and frequency bands. Mechanical stimulation of the periphery increased LFP power relative to spontaneous activity in both awake and anesthetized animals. However, comparisons between awake and anesthetized recordings revealed state-dependent differences in spectral organization. Awake recordings exhibited greater low-frequency (theta-beta) power within the superficial dorsal horn and increased beta-to-high-gamma activity throughout deeper spinal regions. In contrast, anesthetized preparations demonstrated stronger beta-band activity within the deep dorsal horn and intermediate zone, while high-gamma power remained most prominent within the intermediate zone. Together, these findings suggest that behavioral state substantially influences the spectral representation of sensory information within spinal networks.These studies provide one of the first characterizations of intraspinal LFPs in awake, freely behaving animals and establish a framework for future investigations of spinal network dynamics, sensorimotor integration, and circuit reorganization following spinal cord injury.

abstract:
The sensitivity of spinal nociceptive networks to peripheral sensory inputs is tightly regulated by neuromodulatory networks originating in the brainstem. Central to this control is an ascending-descending feedback loop in which ascending spinal projection neurons recruit descending brainstem neurons that in turn regulate segmental nociceptive transmission. It is well established that consciousness, diurnal cycles, physiological stressors, and numerous other factors govern the nature and extent to which these descending controls shape spinal nociceptive transmission. Surprisingly, however, it remains incompletely understood if/how descending nociceptive controls are shaped by anesthesia-induced unconsciousness, despite the ubiquity of pain-related studies using deeply anesthetized preparations.
To address this question, we characterized nociceptive sensory-evoked intraspinal neural activity in vivo in anesthetized rats both before and after complete interruption of descending supraspinal input. All procedures were approved by the WUSTL IACUC. Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats (n=5) were deeply anesthetized with urethane, and microelectrode arrays capable of simultaneously recording from the dorso-ventral extent of the spinal gray matter were implanted into the lumbar enlargement. Neural activity was recorded while inducing natural noxious and innocuous cutaneous feedback from the periphery, as well as during periods in which overt sensory feedback was absent (i.e., spontaneous activity). Data acquisition spanned both before and following a complete spinal transection at T8.
Our primary outcome measures were derived from multi-unit spiking activity and intraspinal local field potentials (LFPs). Multi-unit outcomes focused on changes in sensory-evoked discharge rate the spatial extent of activation, while LFP-based outcomes focused on changes in spectral power and density. We found that multi-unit responsiveness to nociceptive sensory inputs was greater after transection than before. Acute transection also produced region-specific spectral reorganization of LFPs. Theta power increased throughout the spinal cord, alpha power increased in the superficial dorsal horn, and beta power increased in the deep dorsal horn and intermediate zone, while gamma power decreased in the dorsal horn, was unchanged in the intermediate zone, and decreased in the ventral horn. Together, these findings are consistent with the presence of a tonic descending inhibition and/or the preservation of ascending/descending feedback controls even under anesthesia.

abstract: Somatosensory signals from visceral end organs such as the urinary bladder are relayed to the spinal cord, yet the spinal mechanisms that process bladder sensation and coordinate voiding remain largely unclear. Here we identified a subpopulation of Trpc4-expressing interneurons in the lumbosacral dorsal gray commissure that are important for bladder sensation, pain, and micturition. Using a cell-type-specific genetic ablation approach, we found that these neurons regulate both bladder pain and lower urinary tract function. Selective ablation of these neurons increased visceral hypersensitivity and altered voiding, producing more frequent, small-volume voids without affecting bowel output or somatic paw sensation, indicating a bladder-specific role. Simultaneous cystometry and external urethral sphincter electromyography in male mice showed that ablation disrupted the normal coordination of the sphincter during voiding: although the sphincter still engaged, the robustness of its bursting during micturition was degraded, consistent with impaired voiding. To define how these neurons are embedded in the micturition circuit, we used anterograde and monosynaptic retrograde viral tracing to map their inputs and outputs, revealing convergent input from supraspinal micturition centers including the ventromedial medulla and Barrington's nucleus. Together, these results establish this spinal Trpc4 population as an important node for encoding bladder pain and coordinating voiding, providing valuable insight into spinal processing of bladder sensory information and a potential target for visceral pain and voiding disorders.

abstract: To make sense of visual input, the brain must segment scenes into an organized representation of object surfaces. A prominent segmentation signal in primate visual cortex is provided by border ownership neurons. These neurons signal which side of a border in their classical receptive field (cRF) is foreground. We recently found that macaque cortical Area V4 contains columnar clusters of border ownership neurons. An important open question is the relation between these neurons and perception, because no study has recorded from them during a scene segmentation task. Here we address this gap by using a novel paradigm to compare border ownership signals with the animal’s percept on a trial-by-trial basis. We designed a stimulus in which two abutting surfaces compete for ownership of a common border. We manipulated the ambiguity of border ownership by varying relative depth using binocular disparity: the surface that is near relative to the other surface owns the common border. We kept the common border horizontal, such that it did not carry depth information. We trained a male macaque to report the side of foreground by making a saccade to one of two choice targets. To decorrelate the perceptual choice from the saccade vector, we randomly varied the position of the choice targets between trials. During the task we recorded from single and multiunits in V4 using Neuropixels probes, positioning the scenes such that only the common border overlapped with the cRFs. The monkey's choice varied systematically with relative depth, yielding a smooth psychometric function. V4 units were often strongly tuned for the polarity of depth across the common border (thus border ownership). We compared the tuning of individual units with the animal’s percept by computing choice probabilities (CP, the probability that the firing rate for a choice in favor of the unit’s preferred side of ownership is larger than that for the opposite choice) for a fixed, ambiguous scene. We find a larger number of border ownership units with statistically significant CP than expected by chance, and for most of these, the prediction of choice is consistent with the preferred side of border ownership (CP > 0.5). Finally, we find that random forest classifiers trained on spike counts to unambiguous scenes from all simultaneously recorded units in a penetration can separate trials with opposite choices for ambiguous scenes better than expected by chance (area under the ROC curve > 0.5). Together, our data suggest that border ownership signals in V4 predict perception in a scene segmentation task.

abstract: The lightness of a surface is poorly predicted by its luminance, and instead strongly determined by visual context. The underlying neural process of context integration is poorly understood. Low-level theories propose a contrast-like computation, whereas mid-level theories propose that the visual system parses scenes into regions of approximately constant illumination, which then guide the computation of lightness. We recently identified "lightness clusters" in macaque visual cortical Area V4 — columns of neurons that show a net lightness bias in their representation of the local luminance (Didehvar et al., 2025). Here, we investigate how lightness clusters integrate visual context.We recorded from single- and multiunits in V4 of one macaque using Neuropixels probes. After mapping the classical receptive fields (cRFs), we presented checkerboard scenes with spatially varying illumination, to identify lightness clusters as in our recent work. We then presented Noisy Argyle scenes (Kim et al., 2018; more than 5000 unique scenes per session) while the animal was fixating a small target. These scenes are derived from the Argyle illusion, in which alternating illumination bands have a strong effect on surface lightness (Adelson, 2000). Noisy Argyle scenes were generated by adding an independent sample of Gaussian luminance noise to distinct scene elements, but not to the square in which the cRFs were positioned. Spike-triggered averaging revealed individual units that were mostly influenced by scene elements in the illumination band that contained the cRFs, and mostly close to the cRFs. To investigate if this pattern is relevant at the population level, we developed a cross-condition decoding approach. We trained random forest regressors on population spike counts to checkerboard responses to decode the luminance in the cRFs. We then used these decoders to decode luminance from the Noisy Argyle responses. We identified the scene elements that significantly influenced the decoded luminance by comparing the groups of scenes with resp. the lowest and the highest decoded luminance. In lightness clusters we find that these scene elements were clustered similar to the pattern of single units (permutation test p<0.05, 2 penetrations). In a third penetration which was not a lightness cluster, the pattern did not respect the illumination borders. Together our data suggest that the representation of luminance in lightness clusters is mostly influenced by patches in the same illumination band (as predicted by mid-level theories), but dependent on distance (as predicted by low-level theories), consistent with human psychophysics (Kim et al., 2018).

abstract:
Low arousal reduces performance in attention, decision making, and reasoning tasks differently across individuals. Supported by coordinated activity across large-scale brain networks, functional connectivity (FC) is useful for examining how neural co-activation changes with arousal. While most fMRI research shows strengthened sensory/motor FC during low arousal, these studies primarily rely on group-level inferences. This obscures meaningful individual differences, limiting the ability to capture nuanced, participant-specific patterns. Here, we use a precision mapping approach to uncover reliable individual signatures of arousal-related FC changes hidden in group-level analyses. We ran two analyses: (1) a group-level analysis of participants with >5 minutes of fMRI data (N = 40, F = 30, μage = 24.4, σage = 4.1), and (2) a precision analysis of subjects with >20 minutes of data (N = 3, F = 2, μage = 30.3, σage = 4.4).
Participants rated arousal for each resting-state scan on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = high, 7 = low). On average, participants completed 29.72 resting-state scans across 4 sessions. Only high (1-2) and low (6-7) arousal runs were kept. fMRI data was preprocessed to align images, denoised, then parcellated into 300 regions of interest (ROI) using the Seitzman atlas. Pearson’s pairwise correlations were computed between the averaged ROI time series for each subject. Between subjects, FC matrices were averaged within each condition and compared. We used the Network-Based Statistic to test for significant differences in FC across group conditions.
Group-level results showed increased FC in the dorsal sensorimotor network consistent with prior work (t(38) = 4.50, NBS-corrected p < 0.001). Precision mapping revealed previously obscured arousal patterns where low arousal was characterized by increased fronto-parietal and decreased auditory network FC. Precision fMRI may reveal stable individual neural correlates of low arousal, allowing targeted care for populations struggling with diminished arousal.

abstract: Graph metrics are used to quantify characteristics of functional brain networks. They are typically computed from 10-minute runs of fMRI data per subject. Reproducibility within individuals is key for detecting meaningful differences in brain network organization that might relate to clinical characteristics. Precision mapping studies that collect large amounts of high-quality data per individual have revealed that estimates of graph metrics such as global efficiency and participation coefficient vary with data quantity, often requiring more than what is commonly collected to be reliable. Yet the reliability of a broader range of graph metrics across data lengths remains to be systematically characterized. Here, we analyze the reliability of a wide range of graph metrics using precision mapping fMRI data from N=87 subjects with more than 80 minutes of data each. Data were preprocessed, denoised, and parcellated into 300 regions of interest using the Seitzman atlas. Pearson correlations were computed between averaged ROI time series. Connectivity matrices were proportionally thresholded at 9 densities ranging from 2% to 10%. We find that: (1) only a subset of metrics reaches 0.8 reliability even with 15-60 min of data (depending on the metric). This subset includes functional connectivity, degree, strength, global efficiency, participation coefficient, and closeness centrality; (2) thresholds have mixed effects, strongly influencing clustering coefficient, local efficiency, modularity, closeness centrality, and integration-segregation difference, while having little impact on other metrics. These findings demonstrate that data quantity critically affects graph metric reliability and may influence the interpretation of differences in brain network organization if data quality and quantity are not carefully controlled, with implications for fMRI studies using graph metrics to derive individual characteristics of brain networks relevant for clinical understanding.
