abstract: Dopamine signaling has been primarily studied in the striatum, leaving its functions in other brain regions poorly understood despite widespread dopaminergic innervation. Although dopamine is required for long-term memory in the hippocampus, technical challenges in directly measuring dopamine release during behavior have left the source and role of hippocampal dopamine signals unresolved. Using simultaneous optical dopamine measurement and temporally precise, physiologically titrated optogenetic manipulation during behavior, we identify substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) as a major source of reward-associated dopamine transients in dorsal CA1. In a hidden reward zone task, these transients were tightly coupled to rewarded licking bouts, consistent with an action-related signal at reward collection. We hypothesized that this signal reinforces reward-related information during learning. Brief suppression of SNc dopaminergic inputs during the post-reward period reduced the dopamine transient and impaired memory for goal location tested 24 hr later, demonstrating the necessity of this signal. Control manipulations delivered earlier on the track or during dark time had no effect. Conversely, boosting SNc dopamine release at rewards augmented reward transients and enhanced next day memory. Together, these findings identify a surprising role for SNc dopaminergic action signals in reinforcing hippocampal reward-related information during the formation of long-term memories. Furthermore, these discoveries suggest a potential circuit link between the loss of hippocampal SNc dopaminergic inputs and the cognitive impairment often seen in Parkinson's disease.

abstract:
Every brain must adapt to an unpredictable world, yet individuals differ in how readily they learn. Theoretical work in neuroscience and machine learning suggests that learning is fastest when a system is initialized close to instability — i.e., near criticality — because such systems support a diverse repertoire of patterns and multi-scale correlations that promote information propagation.
Here, we empirically estimate an individual's distance to criticality and ask whether it predicts subsequent motor learning. In adult WT mice (N=18), we recorded single-unit activity in primary motor cortex for 24-48 hours in the baseline period. Then, we exposed mice to two six-day motor tasks: prey capture and ladder crossing. Using a renormalization-group-based measure of proximity to criticality (d2), we found that mice closer to criticality learned both tasks faster (prey capture: r²=0.74; ladder gait acquisition: r²=0.61), even though d2 predicted neither naive performance nor asymptotic skill. Thus, d2 a specific predictive power on learning rate. Mice closer to criticality also paired a broader repertoire of ladder-crossing exploration with a more tightly consolidated successful gait, linking criticality to the explore-exploit tradeoff during skill acquisition. In the visual cortex of anesthetized ferret kits (N=14), baseline d2 also predicted the magnitude of experience-dependent shifts in direction selectivity following patterned visual stimulation (r²=0.54), exceeding all comparator features. A minimal recurrent network model reproduces these effects: proximity to criticality sets the timescale over which a system can assign credit to past experience, directly setting the rate of learning. Together, these results show that proximity to criticality can account for the capacity to learn, from artificial networks to the mammalian brain.

abstract: The critical catecholamine norepinephrine (NE) is produced by small populations of noradrenergic cells located in the brainstem, sympathetic chain, and adrenal medulla. Despite their limited numbers, these cells have an outsized impact on diverse behaviors and physiological drives, including arousal, stress responses, and autonomic function. Dysregulation of NE synthesis in the locus coeruleus, the largest population of noradrenergic neurons in the brain, has been implicated in numerous psychiatric, neurodevelopmental, and neurodegenerative disorders, highlighting the importance of understanding the regulation of NE synthesis. Identifying factors that contribute to variations in NE levels are crucial for identifying vulnerabilities to neurological disorders and may reveal novel therapeutic targets. The enzyme responsible for the final step in NE synthesis is dopamine β-hydroxylase, encoded by the DBH gene, which catalyzes the conversion of dopamine to NE. Our lab generated a floxed allele of mouse Dbh which unexpectedly exhibited reduced Dbh mRNA levels in both central and peripheral noradrenergic cells in the absence of Cre recombination. NE was also reduced in the brain, but not in the adrenal medulla or plasma. Sequence analysis indicates that the insertion of a loxP site in intron 1 of Dbh interrupted an evolutionarily conserved sequence element located within a larger putative enhancer that is present in both mouse and human DBH genes. We employed CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) and ATAC-seq in Dbh-expressing mouse neuroblastoma cells to assess the activity of this putative enhancer region and further characterize its capacity to regulate Dbh transcription. We found that CRISPRi of sequences within the conserved region significantly decreased Dbh and induced a closed chromatin conformation at the target site. Similar targeting of the orthologous region in human neuroblastoma cells significantly reduced DBH mRNA and protein expression, demonstrating an evolutionarily conserved role for this enhancer in regulating DBH expression. Together, these findings identify a conserved genetic regulatory element that influences DBH expression and may contribute to individual variation in NE synthesis. Ongoing studies are investigating the functional consequences of enhancer perturbation on NE production, the broader chromatin landscape and transcriptional networks influenced by this regulatory element, and the capacity of enhancer activation to increase DBH expression. Future work will also examine whether known genetic variants within this conserved region alter DBH expression and contribute to altered NE synthesis.

abstract: The gut microbiome plays an important role in human metabolism, nutrition, physiology, and immune function. Accumulating evidence suggests that imbalances in the normal gut microbiome are linked to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) through the regulation of microbiome-associated metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). These findings suggest that reconditioning the gut microbiome may represent a novel strategy for treating the disease.Soluble dietary fiber (SDF) is a fermentable carbohydrate found in plant-based foods that cannot be digested by human enzymes in the small intestine. However, once SDF reaches the large intestine, it can be selectively metabolized by the gut microbiota. Additionally, recent studies have indicated that Apolipoprotein E genotype (APOE) genotype, the strongest common genetic risk factor for AD, influences the structure of the gut microbiome. This raises the question of whether APOE isoforms differentially influence the impact of SDF intake on metabolism, immunity, and brain function synergistically with the gut microbiota.Here, we tested whether soluble dietary fiber could modulate gut microbiome composition and associated metabolite production in an APOE genotype-dependent manner. Mice expressing human APOE3 or APOE4 were randomly assigned to two dietary groups and fed either custom SDF-free or -rich diets for 1.5 months beginning at 2 months of age. Targeted metabolomic analysis revealed that the main SCFAs—acetate, propionate, and butyrate—were significantly higher in APOE4 mice than in APOE3 mice across diet types. (genotype effect, p < 0.05). Propionate and butyrate levels were also significantly higher in mice fed the SDF-rich diet compared with those fed the SDF-free diet (diet-type effect, p < 0.05). Additionally, 16S rRNA-based microbiome analysis revealed microbial community shifts associated with both diet type and genotype. E.g., Romboutsia ilealis was significantly more abundant in mice fed the SDF-free diet than in those fed the SDF-rich diet, whereas Erysipelotrichaceae Allobaculum was significantly more abundant in mice fed the SDF-rich diet than in those fed the SDF-free diet. Both taxa were more abundant in APOE4 mice than in APOE3 mice.Currently, we are evaluating factors involved in neuroinflammation and other brain functions and attempting to integrate these findings with microbiome and metabolome data to provide a holistic understanding of these complex interactions. Finally, we will discuss the implications of these findings for AD and future directions.

abstract:
Modulation of high-frequency activity (HFA) underlies many cognitive processes, in particular selective attention. Attention in general provides salient signals to investigate the larger question of how different cortical and subcortical brain regions interact during cognitive processes. A particular feature of interest is that HFA, even when observed across large cortical regions, tends to be phase-locked to low-frequency rhythms, particularly in the theta (4-8 Hz) range. However, the mechanisms underlying this synchronization of HFA across distributed brain regions remain unclear, especially in the cases of cortical areas that only have weak direct connections. We hypothesize that higher-order thalamic nuclei—especially the pulvinar—play a key role in coordinating this long-range synchronization by entraining outgoing signals to separate cortical regions through theta-band oscillations.
Here, we approach this question in intracranial recordings in humans. We analyzed cortical and thalamic responses from intracranial electrodes implanted in 12 epilepsy patients while they performed a visual spatial attention task (i.e. Egly-Driver task) where visual cues signaled the likely location of upcoming targets. We preprocessed this data using data-driven, clustering-based referencing, which identifies both unique and structurally shared signals in iEEG recordings. We then used a previously described algorithm to identify short-duration, high-amplitude bursts of HFA (which are comparable but use a more general definition than ripples described in the literature).
We observe that both cue and target presentation reliably elicits theta oscillations in the pulvinar and HFA bursts across multiple cortical regions. Furthermore, we find that cortical bursts are significantly phase-locked to the rising phase of pulvinar theta, and that pulvinar theta is stronger when bursts co-occur in multiple regions. We interpret this result as a processing cascade where pulvinar theta is used to synchronize cortical bursts, which in turn reinforce the theta oscillation in thalamus. Additionally, we see that theta phase extracted from different pulvinar subnuclei is locked to bursts in different cortical subnetworks, reflecting underlying thalamocortical connectivity. Finally, we present preliminary results that there is homogeneity among the properties of bursts that may vary depending on the brain region and networks they are a part of. These findings provide novel insight into the role of the thalamus in coordinating cortical activity during attention by leveraging low-frequency oscillations to facilitate inter-areal communication.

abstract: To make sense of the world around us, the visual system must segment complex visual scenes into an organized representation of distinct object surfaces. Scene segmentation signals are prominent in the primate visual cortex. A substantial proportion of neurons in visual cortical Areas V2 and V4 signal border ownership, i.e. which side of a border is owned by a foreground surface. Psychophysics studies suggest that scene segmentation is informed by cues such as contour junctions. A prominent type of contour junction is the T-junction, which is formed where a border of an occluded surface meets that of an occluding surface. The resulting ‘T’ shape is informative about the depth order of the surfaces: the stem of the T points away from the occluding surface. How the visual system represents T-junctions and how these signals relate to the neural representation of border ownership remains poorly understood. Here we investigate this question by directly comparing the neural representation for border ownership and for T-junction orientation. We recorded spike rates from single and multi-units in visual areas V4 and V2 using Neuropixels probes in a male macaque. After measuring the classical receptive fields (cRFs) of the neurons, we presented three types of scenes during passive fixation. First, classical border ownership scenes, in which the cRFs only contained a luminance border which could be owned by a square surface on one or the other side (Square scenes). Second, scenes in which the cRFs only contained an isolated T-junction (Tj-cropped). Third, stimuli in which identical T-junctions as in Tj-cropped scenes were part of a more elaborate scene (a pair of occluding squares; Tj-squares). Each type of scene was presented at 8-12 orientations, and with different possibilities for the contrast polarity across the borders in the scene. We find that a substantial proportion of units are tuned to the orientation of T-junctions in Tj-cropped scenes. We find that the tuning for T-junction orientation is significantly correlated between Tj-cropped and Tj-squares scenes for V2 units, but not for V4 units. In contrast, in V4, and also in V2, we find a significant correlation between the preferred orientation of border ownership between Square scenes and Tj-squares scenes. In neither area we find a significant correlation between the tuning for T-junction orientation in Tj-cropped scenes and border ownership tuning in Square scenes. Together, our data suggest a dissociation in the representation of local and global scene segmentation cues, with a shift in dominance from a more local to a more global representation between V2 and V4.

abstract: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is an established and highly effective treatment for patients with severe depression. However, its mechanisms of action remain incompletely understood, and objective early markers of antidepressant response are still needed. Slow-wave sleep (SWS) plays an important role in synaptic plasticity that may be relevant to antidepressant recovery. We examined whether early changes in SWS during ECT were associated with changes in depression severity. Twenty-two participants undergoing an index course of ECT in an ongoing longitudinal study, DNS-ECT, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05905705, completed overnight sleep EEG recordings and Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) assessments over the course of therapy. We examined whether early change in SWS, measured from baseline to two weeks after ECT initiation as a percentage of total sleep time, was associated with change in depression severity from baseline to the end of the ECT course. To account for potential heterogeneity in treatment response, we used a two-component Gaussian mixture model to identify latent response phenotypes based on changes in SWS and MADRS scores. Within each phenotype, we assessed the association between SWS change and MADRS change using Pearson and Spearman correlations. We then used multiple linear regression to test whether the association between SWS change and MADRS change differed by phenotype. MADRS scores decreased substantially by the end of the ECT course, with a mean reduction of 14.1 points from baseline (paired t = 7.30, p < 0.0001). Mean (SD) SWS increased from 60.0 (54.8) to 83.8 (82.6) minutes (Δ = +24.3 minutes, +6.2 %) from baseline to week 2. The mixture model identified two response phenotypes of similar size (n = 12 and n = 10) that did not differ at baseline in age, sex, MADRS, QIDS, or SWS (all p > 0.30). Within both phenotypes, greater SWS gains were strongly associated with greater MADRS reductions. Phenotype 1 showed a slope of −0.92, Pearson r = −0.86, p = 0.0004; phenotype 2 showed a slope of −0.44, Pearson r = −0.85, p = 0.002. The combined model explained 79% of the variance in MADRS change (overall p < 0.0001). Phenotypes differed in coupling magnitude but not direction (interaction p = 0.024; likelihood-ratio p = 0.012). Early gains in SWS during the first two weeks of ECT were closely coupled to subsequent reductions in depression severity assessed at the end of the ECT course across two latent response phenotypes, supporting a consistent relationship between SWS enhancement and antidepressant response. Larger studies are needed to replicate these findings and identify prospective markers of phenotype membership.

session_title: Computational Models of Decision-Making

abstract: Why do we want to know the future? Humans and many animals pay for information to predict uncertain rewards, even when they cannot control them. The reason for this conserved yet seemingly paradoxical preference - “subjective value without instrumental value” - remains unknown. Here we develop a normative framework to explain the origin of such preferences, their persistence across species, and their contributions to survival. We formalize and evaluate theories that explain information’s subjective value as originating as an adaptive estimate of its advantage for solving core computational problems posed by natural environments. One theory, which we call Time Allocation (TA) theory, proposes that information helps organisms in nature improve their time allocation during foraging (Vasconcelos et al., 2015). A second theory, Credit Assignment (CA) theory, proposes that information helps organisms solve the temporal credit assignment problem during reinforcement learning (Bromberg-Martin and Hikosaka, 2009). We embody each theory with a computational model of an optimal Bayesian agent maximizing reward in a naturalistic environment. We then compute the instrumental value of information in each model, and test whether it predicts the true subjective value of information measured experimentally in humans and monkeys (Bromberg-Martin and Feng et al, 2024). We show that these theories operate through distinct mechanisms, yet remarkably, both make a series of common, correct, detailed predictions about human and animal subjective values. This suggests that organisms may place subjective value on information in order to help them to solve both the TA and CA problems simultaneously in nature. We further leverage our framework to derive novel types of information making it possible to dissociate these theories and test if organisms use a mixture of both to compute their subjective values. Indeed, we show that mixed value computations combining both theories achieve the highest performance across diverse naturalistic environments. Finally, we provide evidence that the theorized benefits of information can also apply to artificial neural network (ANN) agents for reinforcement learning, substantially improving both training speed and performance. Thus, our work provides new evidence that organisms compute the subjective value of information in a manner that is non-instrumental in experimental tasks but is conserved across species and well suited to guide adaptive behavior across a range of natural environments.

abstract: Neuronal bursts, defined as brief epochs of high-frequency spiking, are known to play a key role in the formation of memory engrams in rodents, where they drive synaptic plasticity more effectively than isolated spikes. However, whether burst-driven learning also occurs in humans, and the time scales at which bursts drive plasticity in humans, is not well understood. A central challenge is that human memory unfolds during active vision, as observers shift their gaze to sample visual information every 200-300 milliseconds, making it difficult to know what information a given burst encodes. To study this question, we collected simultaneous gaze and Medial Temporal Lobe (MTL) single-neuron recordings from epilepsy patients while they performed an old/new recognition task on natural scene images. We parsed burst events from the spike trains and aligned them temporally with the observer’s fixations to obtain precise measurements of what information was being sampled during neuronal bursting and relate burst activity directly to memory outcomes. Our analyses revealed that: (1) bursts occur preferentially when the observer fixates novel visual information, suggesting bursting is gated by the stimulus novelty during natural viewing, (2) during encoding, bursts carve ‘attractor-like’ basins in the neural state space to strengthen subsequent reinstatement of the encoding neural state, (3) burst sharpen the geometry of memory representations at the population level, separating competing memories and enhancing stored pattern retrieval. Further, a burst-gated Modern Hopfield Network reproduces these dynamics, recapitulating recognition behavior and revealing burst-gating as a sufficient computational mechanism for memory storage and retrieval. Taken together, these results suggest that bursts act as a fixation time-scale plasticity mechanism that supports one-shot learning of complex visual content during natural visual exploration and point to burst-gated plasticity as a unifying principle linking rodent and human memory research.

abstract:
AI coding agents are entering scientific work yet have mainly been designed and tested for software-engineering tasks. Whether coding agents can reliably analyze and explore complex neuroscience datasets and return trustworthy results is an open question. Rigorous analysis takes more than running code; scientific exploration proceeds through many iterations and field-specific workflows, and interpreting each result properly requires knowledge of the underlying biology, not just skill in data analytics.
To enable autonomous analyses in neuroscience, we first built NeuroAI-Bench, the first benchmark of its kind in the field, which we assembled from published and unpublished datasets and accompanying analyses vetted by human domain experts. It comprises >30 tasks across >15 datasets and >500,000 neurons spanning different species and recording modalities, covering data quality control, inferential analysis, method selection, hypothesis testing, and audit of flawed analyses. Each task specifies a scientific question, the dataset to be used, and the required deliverables, allowing agents to infer suitable methods, controls, and interpretations. Grading of agent performance combines deterministic checks on the outputs with expert rubrics that assess scientific reasoning. In tests of whether off-the-shelf coding tools such as Claude Code and Codex could solve these tasks, we found that they struggled to follow the scientific intent, were harder to steer even with customization efforts, and, when they did produce an answer, left fewer traces of how the results were achieved.
We then built NeuroAI-Agent, an open framework whose execution is restricted to pre-approved analysis tools and workflows that are already accepted in the field. It runs several workflows that are performed by digitized personas from a neuroscience lab. We used different AI agents that respectively play a neuroscientist, a data scientist, a librarian that searches the published literature through vector embeddings, a data engineer that prepares and checks the data, and analysts, statisticians, and reviewers. These personas are stacked to mimic how neuroscientists typically work, down to formulating results and reaching conclusions, and the workflows include predefined cross-specialty iteration loops, such as a neuroscientist agent evaluating a statistician agent's output. Every result carries a full audit trail of how it was produced. On NeuroAI-Bench, this system outperformed off-the-shelf coding tools while adding complete traceability. We intend this work to seed further development toward autonomous, trustworthy, and fully traceable neuroscience analysis at scale.

abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal motor neuron disease (MND) characterized by progressive neurodegeneration and TDP-43 pathology. While transcriptional dysregulation is characteristic of ALS, the post-transcriptional mechanisms that amplify and cause neuronal dysfunction remain poorly understood. We recently studied the role of alternative polyadenylation (APA) as a crucial post-transcriptional mechanism linking TDP-43 dysfunction to MND pathogenesis in neuronal cell models and in ALS postmortem tissue. We found that APA dysregulation drives altered 3′ UTR landscapes and aberrant isoform expression in human neurons. These APA-driven changes impact mRNA stability and subcellular localization of disease-relevant transcripts, underscoring the functional relevance of TDP-43-mediated APA.Building on this work, we are now disentangling post-transcriptional regulation observed in the context of TDP-43 depletion from the changes that are observed in the context of aging and nerve injury. Our preliminary data suggest that APA dysregulation is not only a downstream consequence of TDP-43 pathology, but also a coordinated mechanism by which human neurons respond to injury and normal aging. Using a mouse model of sciatic nerve crush we observed a striking shift towards proximal polyadenylation sites (PASs) (70%) shortly after injury followed by a shift towards distal PASs (77%) during the recovery phase. In a parallel study, we found a global shift towards distal PASs in transdifferentiated (‘aged’) neurons relative to induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived (‘young’) neurons from the same donor fibroblasts, with significant enrichment of RNA binding proteins among the affected genes.These findings position APA as not only a novel layer of post-transcriptional regulation in ALS, but as a key mechanism by which neurons regulate gene expression in response to injury and aging.
